t: is susceptible to impurity. Since the ring is the principal part, and it was made not merely to serve the seal but is a vessel in its own right (Sidrei Taharot 134a).

the threshing sieve (ma'aved), the winnowing fork (mizreh), and the gleaning rake (magov). Implements for separating grain from straw. The ma'aved has few teeth and separates the grain from the coarse straw; the mizreh has more, denser teeth and separates finer waste than the ma'aved; the magov has teeth that are denser and more numerous than the mizreh's, and is used for the final separation of the kernels from the waste (see Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 13:7).
and a comb for the head. A comb for hair.
one of whose teeth was removed and replaced with one of metal. Now all the teeth are of wood except one.
these are susceptible to impurity. Because the wood serves the metal.
so that he can hold it by it. That is, he holds it by the metal knob.
is not susceptible to impurity. For the metal is like a handle that serves the wooden staff.

if he made it so that the ground would not wear away the wood, it is susceptible to impurity. Even though the metal serves the wood, the staff is susceptible to impurity, because the metal causes the wood to last and without it the wood would be consumed; thus the metal is the principal part and the staff is susceptible to impurity (Kesef Mishneh, citing Rabbi Yitzchak ben Reuven).
he made them for ornament. For beauty. [Note: In the Commentary to the Mishnah, Rambam writes and vocalizes the word noy as no'i.]
pipes. Metal tubes.
that he fixed to a staff or a door for ornament. See below 11:24.
until he rubs them with fish skin. Until he rubs them with fish skin in order to smooth them.
he decided not to smooth it. He decided not to sand it but to use the bed as it is.
until he finishes off their rims. Until he completes the rim of the basket and ties it so that it will not come apart.

and trims the ends of the twigs and the small pieces of wood that stick out of the back of the basket. Baskets are woven in a warp-and-weft pattern; at the end of the weaving the ends of the basket are tied, and the small branches protruding outward are cut off.
if the baskets were of date palm. Made of palm branches.
the fibers. The tips of the leaves.
for that is how they are kept. For that is how they are customarily used, and their work is therefore complete.
a basket (kalkalah). A basket.
and he trims what sticks out. The protruding branches.
and finishes the hangers. He finishes making the carrying handles called "hangers."
a cup-holder and a flask-holder. Baskets meant for carrying cups or jugs.
the small baskets (kenonim). A kind of woven basket.
and the kelatot. Thin baskets.
and the large sugim. Very large, tightly woven baskets used for grain or flour.
until he makes two courses along their width. Until he makes a woven rim two rows high.
the receptacle of a sieve or a strainer. A vessel placed beneath the sieve or the strainer to collect the flour (the strainer has larger holes than the sieve - Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 15:4).
a kuppah, once he makes two bands along its width. A kuppah is a large basket, and a band is a binding around the base of the basket.

and an arak, once he makes one band in it. An arak is a wicker vessel in the shape of a long, narrow rectangle (Commentary to the Mishnah 16:3). Because of the size of these vessels, they are used even without a real receptacle, with just one or two turns of the weave, even though he intends to add more to the weave, since it is already fit for use as a vessel holding a smaller quantity, and people sometimes use it in this state too - it is susceptible to impurity.
once he trims the fibers. Once he cuts off the tips of the leaves sticking out of the mat.
and all wicker vessels. Vessels made of wicker, such as baskets (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 20:2).
unfinished wooden vessels. Whose work is not finished and which still need sanding or painting, but whose carving and the making of their receptacle are complete and which are fit for use.
to outline it with a stylus or to even it with a compass. To engrave it using a straight or a curved tool (see Isaiah 44:13 and the commentators there).
to smooth it with an adze. To sand it with a cutting tool.
and it is still unfinished. Its making is not complete.

since it does not lack carving and its hollowing is complete. But if he planned to hollow it to a certain size and has not yet completed it, it is not susceptible to impurity (Babylonian Talmud, Chullin 25a).

it is susceptible to impurity. Smoothing and polishing do not hold it back, since ordinary wooden vessels were not made for show but were plain and cheap (ibid. 25b), and therefore they were considered vessels fit for sale and use even if their finishing was not completed (unlike metal vessels - below 8:1).
except for one of eshkero'a. A kind of smooth, heavy, hard wood of light color (long-leaved eshkero'a), which was highly sought after for making fine vessels and carving.

and it seems to me that bone vessels are like those of eshkero'a, and their unfinished forms are not susceptible to impurity. For bone vessels sell at a high price, and until they are completed they are not fit for sale and their work is not finished (Rashi, Chullin 25b, and see Me'irat Einayim).
a wooden article that has no shape of a vessel. Wood that has not been worked or altered so as to show that it is an object prepared for a particular use.
even though it is used, it is not susceptible to impurity. Use alone does not make it a vessel if it has no vessel shape.

the bakers' long boards on which they arrange the loaves while they are still dough. Wooden boards on which bakers place the loaves before putting them into the oven. Although they are flat wooden articles, they are susceptible to impurity by rabbinic decree (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 15:2), since they have the status of utensils used by people (Tosafot, Chagigah 24b).
with red dye or with saffron. Kinds of red coloring.

a bakers' stand on which they place the water with which they smear the dough. It seems to be a wooden board on which a bowl of water is placed, in which they dip their hands during kneading, to wash them and to smear and smooth the surface of the loaf with water (see Kesef Mishneh, Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 15:2, Tiferet Yisrael, and Mishnah Acharonah there).
and if he enclosed it on its four sides, it becomes impure. If he surrounded it with partitions on four sides it is susceptible to impurity, since it has a receptacle.
if it is open on one side, it is pure. If the partition on one of the sides fell, it is pure, since it no longer has a receptacle.
and the board on which they arrange. The board on which they arrange the baked bread.
the semolina makers. Those who make fine flour for sale.
on which they sift the fine flour. They sift the fine flour over it.
the shovel for grits. A winnowing shovel, a kind of large, square, flat spoon, with which they take beans or other legumes that were ground together with their husks and shake them to separate them.
and that of storehouses is pure. With which they sweep the wheat in a storehouse to make it into a pile.
of winepresses. The place where grapes are trodden.
and of threshing floors. The place where grain is gathered.
that which is made for receiving. To receive things inside it.
and that which is made for gathering with. With which scattered things are gathered into one pile, but which is not used to carry things inside it.
all the hangers. The handles of vessels by which they are hung.
are pure. They are not susceptible to impurity, since they are not considered part of the vessel.
the staff of the inspectors. A staff used for probing and feeling inside a heap of straw in case wheat that is subject to tax is hidden there (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 15:4).
because they assist at the time of work. Because they are helpful during work, to hold the vessel better.
the nevalim of the singers are susceptible to impurity. Skins for song, something like bagpipes (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 15:6).
the nevalim of the Levites with which they play music in the Temple are pure. See the rulings and opinions.
the batnon. A stringed instrument that is rested against the belly, like a guitar.
and the niktemon. The instrument called the oud, also called niktimon, from "one-legged," because the neck of the instrument looks like a wooden leg (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 15:6).
and the erus. A drum made of a round wooden frame with a skin stretched over it, which serves as a seat for the women mourners, who drum on it during the eulogy (ibid.).
a weasel trap. A trap for catching weasels.
a kefifah. A basket.
like the form of a large granary. In the shape of a storehouse.
which does not have the status of a vessel. Because it is not carried about (Ra'avad, Me'irat Einayim), or because it has large holes (Merkevet HaMishneh).
leaves that they weave like a fence around the fruit. They make a kind of temporary basket to cover the fruit they pick in the field.
but if they made a fence of boards, it is susceptible to impurity. When it is made of wicker it endures and is considered a vessel.
a wrap of palm fibers. A covering, something like a bag or box, made of palm leaves.
in which they put the moist fruit. Fresh fruit (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 16:5; Arukh HaShulchan 192:14).
if he puts into it and takes out of it, it becomes impure. Since he uses it the way vessels are used.
but if he cannot take out what is inside it, etc.. Since it is meant for a single use it is not considered a vessel.
and if he had it in mind. To use it regularly.
it is susceptible to impurity. For bone vessels have the same law as wooden vessels.
in a chest, a box, or a cupboard. Which are not susceptible to impurity (above 3:2).
if it is in the way of its receiving. That is, he fixed it in the bottom of the chest, with its opening facing up, and it can receive things inside it.
for it does not receive until the chest is tilted onto its side. It cannot serve for receiving when the chest is standing upright.
it is part of the chest and pure. It is considered part of the wall and not a vessel in its own right.
the akkun. A basket for catching fish.
and the rtov. A device for catching birds.
and a wooden cage are pure. For the cage has gaps between its bars, and the akkun and the rtov have large holes, and they are not receptacles.
the madaf. A kind of trap made of a slab of stone or wood propped on a stick with bait placed beneath it; when the bird or animal comes to eat, the stick falls and the slab drops on the prey.
and the paltzur. A wooden trap for catching birds.
and a dam trap. They would build a dam in the water so that fish would gather there, and then drain the water, leaving the fish behind.

the benches in inns and those of teachers of children. Innkeepers and teachers want to save space, so they use a collapsible bench made of legs and a wooden board with holes that serves as the seat. When needed they insert the legs into the holes in the seat, and afterwards they take them apart.
even though they are perforated and they insert the legs into them, they are pure. For they are not joined permanently, and so they are not considered vessels.
if one of its legs was of stone, it is not susceptible to impurity. Since it cannot stand without the stone, the whole bench is considered a stone vessel, which is not susceptible to impurity.
and its form and its use were ruined. It was broken in such a way that it no longer has a form and cannot be used for what it served before it was broken.
all household vessels. Vessels for household use that are not meant for a particular task and into which different things are put each time.
once the vessel is perforated to the size that lets a pomegranate out. Once the vessel has a hole of a size through which a pomegranate could fall out.

neither small nor large, according to the opinion of the one who sees it. The way to estimate what is called a medium pomegranate is by the estimate of the observer. There is no need to check precisely what the average size of pomegranates is.

and there are three pomegranates in the vessel held against one another. When the vessel is full, the crowding holds the pomegranates in place and a larger hole is needed for a pomegranate to fall out of the vessel; conversely, when the vessel is empty a smaller hole suffices for a pomegranate to fall out of it. The measure of the hole that renders the vessel pure is that when there are three pomegranates in the vessel, one of them can fall out (Rabbi Yitzchak ben Reuven; see other explanations in the Ra'avad).
even though it is stopped up. And it never had a hole of the size that lets a pomegranate out.
pure, for a new face has been made for it. It is treated as if the old vessel was broken and a new vessel was made, pure of its old impurity, but susceptible to impurity from now on.
and the saddle-pad of camels. A basket made like a net of thick ropes that is placed on a camel.

and the afifiyorot. A net made of reeds on which vines are trained, and sometimes a vessel is made from it for holding large things such as loaves of bread, which do not fall through even when the vessel has large holes. The way the vessel is made is explained in the next halachah.

afifiyorot to which he added reeds above and below to strengthen them are pure. Afifiyorot are nets made of reeds and have no vessel shape; even if he attached more reeds to make the net denser and stronger, this is not regarded as making a vessel and it is not susceptible to impurity.
if he made sides for it, of any size. If he made walls for it of any height, with the net as the bottom of the vessel.

even though it is all perforated to the size that lets a pomegranate out, it is susceptible to impurity. By means of the sides a vessel shape was made, and so it is susceptible to impurity despite the large holes.
all vessels that cannot hold pomegranates. Because they are small and a pomegranate cannot be put inside them.
such as the rova. A measuring vessel of a quarter of a kav (about 350 cc).
and the small kenonim. Small baskets.
their measure is the size that lets an olive out. If a hole is made in them through which an olive can fall out, they are pure.
their rims were worn away. The walls of the vessel were reduced and cut down.
the bread baskets. Those that are designated for this use.
their measure is loaves of bread. For as long as they can hold bread, they are fit for their purpose.
the gardeners' basket. A basket of vegetable growers.
and that of householders, the size that lets out straw. That is, larger than a bundle of vegetables (Tiferet Yisrael, Kelim 17:1), because householders also use the basket for straw.
and of bath attendants. Those who bring firewood for heating the bathhouse.
with gevavah. Straw mixed with dung, used as fuel.
a bowl box that no longer holds bowls. A box for bowls that was perforated or broken so that bowls cannot be placed in it.
since it holds the large dishes. Since large bowls can be placed in it.

it is susceptible to impurity. Since it serves a task similar to the one it served before it broke, it is still considered a vessel, and its use is not nullified until it breaks to the point that it can no longer hold large dishes (Arukh HaShulchan 194:4).
and likewise a chamber-pot that no longer holds liquids. A pot for relieving oneself that was perforated, so that urine runs out through the hole.

since it holds excrement, it is susceptible to impurity. Since excrement does not escape through the hole, the vessel is susceptible to impurity because it serves a task similar to its original purpose (see there).
any wooden vessel that split into two. That broke into two pieces.

even though they hold on their sides, like pans. Even when the fragments can still be used as receptacles - for example, an alpas (a kind of frying pan) with deep sides, whose fragments can still be used as receptacles even after it breaks - nevertheless they are not susceptible to impurity, because they no longer serve their original purpose (compare below 18:10).
a folding table. A collapsible table made of two parts.
and like the tamchui mizvon, which is made entirely of compartments. A large wooden dish with small bowls inside it, made of one piece with the large dish.

and likewise a cup-holder and a flask-holder. A vessel built of a board with compartments in which small jugs or cups are placed; the case here is a vessel that has three compartments (Chasdei David, Kelim, Bava Metzia 6:8).
if one of them was damaged. One compartment broke and can no longer be used.

the one that was damaged is pure, and is not joined to the other compartments. The damaged compartment is considered a vessel in its own right and does not become impure even if impurity touched the intact compartments (compare below 13:14).
if the second was damaged, it is pure and is not joined to it. To the compartment that remained intact.
a mashpelet. A tall, large basket for carrying manure out to the fields or for straw (Mishnah, Kelim 24:9).
whose middle is high and whose corners slope down. It is divided into two parts by a partition in the middle, and the partition is higher than the walls.
and was damaged on one side. One of the walls broke.
it is impure, because it holds on the other side. Because the other part can serve as a receptacle by means of the partition in the middle.
if it was damaged on the second side, it is pure. For no side remains in it that is fit for use.
the table. A small table for personal use, round, with three legs.
and the dulpeki. A table on which foods and drinks are arranged, and from which the food is served to the guests' individual tables (Commentary to the Mishnah, Avodah Zarah 5:5).

that were damaged. Parts of the table broke off and are missing, but its legs are still joined to one another and the remaining part can stand (see another explanation in Rav Ovadiah of Bartenura, Kelim 22:1).
until they split and each part is separated from the other. It broke into two parts, one of which has a leg attached, and then the table cannot stand.
if one of their legs was removed, they are pure. A table cannot stand on two legs and cannot be used.
if the third leg was removed. And only the board remained.

if he had in mind that he would eat on this table... as one eats from a tablet, they are susceptible to impurity. If he intended to use the board as a tray for eating, it is susceptible to impurity, since by the intention it becomes a different vessel (see below 8:10).
wicker vessels. Woven wicker vessels such as baskets.
whose rims fell off. The upper part of the wall, where they are bound, fell off; they are pure, because once the binding comes apart, the whole vessel is bound to come apart.
and if any of the binding of their rims remained, they are susceptible to impurity. If any part of the bound rim remained, the vessel is susceptible to impurity.
a tablet (tavlah). A flat wooden board that can serve as a tray and is susceptible to impurity.
which he filled with wood and fixed in place. That he attached pieces of wood to it with a permanent attachment.
pure. It can no longer serve as a tray, and the name of vessel is annulled from it.

if he covered it with boards, it is susceptible to impurity. If he covered the pieces of wood he had fixed in place with a uniform covering of straight boards, it is again susceptible to impurity, because it can again serve its function (Chasdei David, Kelim, Bava Batra 1:9).

a bench that came apart is pure; if he wove it with straps or ropes, it is susceptible to impurity. The bench is made of a board used for sitting, joined to two legs by nails. If the legs came apart from the bench, it is pure. But if he attached the legs with ropes, the bench again becomes susceptible to impurity.

the camel baskets. Nets that have no vessel shape; when one wants to use them, one ties them around the goods one wants to carry in them, and the shape of a basket forms; when one wants to take out the goods, one unties the net and the goods fall out, and the basket goes back to being a shapeless net.
that he covered with marble and left room for placing cups. He covered them with marble but left an uncovered place in which to put the cups.

whether with a standing covering. A permanent covering fastened with nails and the like that cannot be removed (Rashi, Chagigah 26b). Some explain it as a covering that can stand on its own without needing the thing it covers (Otzar HaGeonim there; see Tosafot there).
whether he covered its rim. A lizbaz is a molding, a projecting frame around the table.
or did not cover its rim. Even if he did not cover them, the table is considered entirely covered.
eshkero'a. See above 5:1.
since he covered all of them. The whole vessel is covered.
are pure, as we have explained. Above 4:4, that a covered vessel is not susceptible to impurity.
the turmel. A pouch, a leather bag.
until he finishes off its rims. Until he folds over the edge of the pouch and sews it.
and trims the small knobs sticking out of the back of the hide. He cuts off the small protrusions sticking out of the edge.
its straps. The leather thongs used to close the vessel.
a skurtia. A leather mat that serves as a tablecloth for eating.
and he makes its tzitzit. A circle of leather with decorations that is sewn into the middle of the mat for ornament.
a ketavlia. A leather mat spread over a bed.
once he finishes the box. The square of the tefillin.

even though he is yet to put the strap into it, it is susceptible to impurity. For the box is already a finished vessel, and the strap is needed for the sake of the mitzvah and not to complete the making of the vessel (Chasdei David, Kelim, Bava Batra 4:1).
the leather of the cradle. A hide that is placed in a baby's cradle so that he will not soil the bedding.
for he is going to make a navel for it. To attach to it a small ball for the baby to play with (Commentary of the Vilna Gaon on the Tosefta, Kelim, Bava Metzia 6:1).
the sandal, once he fastens it. Once he ties the sandal's straps (Chasdei David, Kelim, Bava Metzia 6:1).

the shoe, once he dries it on the last. The last is a mold of wood or leather in the shape of a foot. The way a shoe is made is that the leather is soaked in water to make it easy to work, then the shoe is shaped on the last and left on it to dry; from the moment the shoe is dry its work is finished and it is susceptible to impurity.
and if he is going to dye them and mark them with lines. To color the shoe or to draw decorations on it.
until he dyes them and until he marks them with lines. For these actions are part of the work of making the shoe.
leather that has no shape of a vessel. A shapeless piece of leather, not cut to measure for any task (see below 23:3).

and likewise the leather with which they gather cattle dung. A piece of leather used for gathering animal dung, or which is tied behind an animal so that the dung does not fall on the grain (see Commentary to the Mishnah and Tiferet Yisrael, Kelim 16:7).
and the leather with which they muzzle an animal's mouth. Which they tie over its mouth so that it will not eat from the grain.
and the leather with which they drive off the bees when they take the honey. On which they light a fire so that the smoke will drive away the bees.
and the leather with which they fan the wind because of the heat. A fan.
every finger-sheath. A piece of leather into which the fingers are put, open at both ends and without a receptacle (Tiferet Yisrael, Kelim 26:3).
except that of fruit-gatherers. Those who gather fruit for drying.

because it holds the og, it is impure. The og is a wild shrub on which grow clusters of small red fruits (sumac). The fruit-gatherers' practice is that when they find og fruits they put them inside the finger-sheath leather (Rav Shimshon and Tiferet Yisrael there).
if it does not hold most of the og. Perhaps this means most of the fruits in an average cluster of og.
the leather belt. A belt made of leather.
and the leathers that amputees sew onto their knees. Leathers that people with amputated legs sew onto their knees in order to walk on them.
and likewise leathers made like rings, etc.. Craftsmen roll up their clothes while working and put on their hands leather rings that keep the garment from falling back down.
are susceptible to impurity like the other plain leather vessels. For their impurity is rabbinic (above 1:10).
threshing-floor winnowers. Those who winnow grain on the threshing floor and use leather to hold the winnowing fork firmly.
and that of travelers. Who hold a staff or protect their hands from thorns (Tosafot Yom Tov, Kelim 16:6).
and that of flax workers. Who beat the flax and protect their hands from being hurt by the thorns and splinters mixed in the flax.
and if it was that of dyers and smiths. Who use leather so that the sweat of their hands will not harm the article they are working on.

anything made as a receptacle, so that a thorn will not strike him and so that he can hold well, is susceptible to impurity. If the purpose of the leather is to protect the hand, it is like a receptacle made to receive the hand.
and that made because of sweat... is not susceptible to impurity. If the purpose of the leather is to protect against sweat, it is not made as a receptacle for the hand.

once it is perforated to the size that lets out spools of warp. Balls of rolled warp threads. Warp threads are thinner than weft threads, so when warp and weft threads of equal length are rolled, the ball formed from the warp thread is smaller.
if it cannot hold warp. If the skin was originally made so that it cannot hold spools of warp.
since it holds weft, it is susceptible to impurity. Because it is fit to hold spools of weft it is considered a vessel and is susceptible to impurity.

until most of it is perforated. Since it was originally made with large holes, it does not become pure when the hole widens and it can no longer hold spools of weft, but only when most of it is perforated (Chasdei David, Kelim, Bava Metzia 6:6; Sidrei Taharot, Kelim 159b).
the skin bag (chemet). A leather waterskin, usually used for liquids.
the turmel. A leather pouch that has an inner compartment for placing small objects.
whose inner pocket was damaged. The inner compartment tore.
the turmel is still susceptible to impurity. For it is still intact and can hold various objects.
and it is not joined to it. If impurity touched the pocket that was damaged, the turmel does not become impure, and if the turmel became impure, the pocket touching it does not become impure.

a skin bag whose testicles receive along with it. A skin bag made from the hide of a whole animal, such that when the hide is flayed, two small pockets protruding from the skin bag are formed from the place of the testicles.
and they were damaged. They were perforated.

pure, for they do not receive in their usual way. Although he can tie the mouth of the skin bag and fill it through the testicles, the testicles are pure, because when the skin bag is filled from its mouth the testicles do not receive the liquid.
and shenatzot. Straps or laces that go through loops.
an amki sandal. A sandal worn in valleys and plains, made of straps that are tightened on the foot.

and a pouch with laces. A pouch (purse) that has loops into which laces are inserted and tied to close the pouch. The shape of the pouch is formed by tightening the laces and not by sewing, so when the laces are removed, the leather returns to its flat shape.

these are susceptible to impurity when they are loosened... and likewise if they became impure and he removed the laces from them and their shape was ruined, they are pure. The commentators found this halachah difficult, because it is not clear what the difference is between the first case, in which they are susceptible to impurity when loosened, and the second case, in which they are pure. Some explained that at the beginning of the halachah the case is one where the laces are not tightened but are still inside the loops, and at the end the case is one where the laces were removed entirely, and then the vessel is pure (Kiryat Sefer; Mayim Tehorim, Kelim 26:1; Chasdei David, Kelim, Bava Metzia 1:7). Others explained that in the first part the laces slipped out on their own, and in the last part the person removed the laces from the pouch deliberately, thereby showing that he nullifies it from being a vessel (Arukh HaShulchan 196:17; Mishnah Acharonah, Kelim 26:1). Others explained it in other ways (Sidrei Taharot, Kelim 230a; Chazon Ish, Kelim 30:4).

a pouch with laces whose laces were removed, etc.. It seems that this case qualifies the previous halachah: when the leather did not flatten out upon the removal of the laces but kept the shape of a receptacle, it is still susceptible to impurity (Mayim Tehorim, Kelim 26:1).
if it flattened and became plain leather, it is pure. As explained in the previous halachah.
if he sewed a patch onto it from below. He sewed a piece of cloth onto it to serve as a lining for the vessel.
it is susceptible to impurity even though it is flat, since it has the shape of a vessel. The sewn cloth shows that this is not mere leather but leather prepared as a vessel.
and leather on which an amulet was written is pure. It is not considered a vessel.

and if he cut some of it and made a link for an ornament, it is susceptible to impurity. Although it is among the plain leather vessels, the Sages decreed impurity on it as an ornament (Chasdei David, Kelim, Bava Metzia 1:14).
the head tefillin are four vessels. It has four compartments, called boxes.

and he undid the first box and repaired it, it is a primary source of impurity as it was. The tefillin are not regarded as a new vessel, since parts of the original compartments, which are impure as a primary source of impurity, remain in it; therefore the entire tefillin and all its compartments are impure at the level of a primary source of impurity.

if he also undid the fourth and repaired it, the whole becomes a first-degree impurity, etc.. Since all the compartments were taken apart and put back, the tefillin are regarded as a new vessel that touched the old tefillin, which were a primary source of impurity, and so their impurity is of the level of first degree.
if he again undid the first a second time and repaired it. After he took apart and restored all the compartments, he took apart the first compartment of the tefillin once more and repaired it.
it is a first-degree impurity as it was. The tefillin remain at the level of first degree, because the compartments that were not replaced are still impure.

if he again undid the fourth as well and repaired it, the whole is pure, for a first-degree impurity does not make vessels impure. Now all the compartments have been replaced, and it is as though new tefillin were made that touched the old tefillin. That touch does not make them impure at all, because a first-degree impurity does not make vessels impure.
as we have explained. Hilchot Tumat Met 5:7-8.
and likewise a sandal that is a midras impurity. That a zav stepped on, and it is a primary source of impurity.
and was cut. Was cut off.
one of its ears. The holes into which the straps are inserted to tie the sandal to the foot; the sandal does not become pure as long as one ear remains attached.
but it is impure by contact with midras. As though it had touched a midras, and it becomes a first-degree impurity.

if he did not manage to repair the first before the second was cut... it is pure. Then the sandal is entirely pure, and if he repairs it, it is a completely new vessel that did not touch the old sandal.
or its heel strap was cut. The strap that holds the heel.
or its nose was removed. The strap that holds the front of the foot.

a shoe that was damaged, etc.. A shoe is not open on top like a sandal, and its purpose is to cover the foot. Therefore if it was damaged and does not cover most of the foot, it is pure (Sidrei Taharot, Kelim 233a).
that of the hand. Which is made of one square box.
once he cuts it on three sides. He cuts the tefillin box at the place of its connection to the titura (the wide lower square) on three sides.
and that of the head. Which is built of four compartments, so that each compartment is attached both to the titura and to the compartment next to it.
and the stuffing. See above 5:1. The stuffed form discussed here is made of leather with filling inside.
that tore after they became impure. The case is where the seam closing the opening for the filling tore; because the receptacle is still intact, they remain impure (Tiferet Yisrael, Kelim 23:1).
and what is inside them is pure. The filling is not part of the vessel and did not become impure with it.
the saddle. A riding saddle, which is stitched from side to side so that the thread connects the cloths that fill the saddle.
unfinished metal vessels. Vessels whose work is not finished.
anything he is going to file. To smooth.
or to polish. To remove the filings produced by the filing (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 11:3). Some explain that it means to make gold settings for ornament (Rashi, Chullin 25b).
or to scrape. To remove bumps left after the filing (Commentary to the Mishnah, ibid.). Some explain that filing silver and gold vessels is called scraping (Rashi, ibid.).
or to burnish. To polish.
or to strike with a hammer. To straighten the vessel.
or that lacked a handle. A grip.
or a neck. A neck for the vessel, the narrow part of the jar.

it is not susceptible to impurity until he repairs it and beautifies it and no work at all remains in it. Metal vessels are not considered finished until they are beautified and completely finished, because they are made for show or because they sell at a high price (Babylonian Talmud, Chullin 25b).
the iron ingot (esht). Iron ore that has not been smelted and refined.
the metal cake (chararah). A lump of molten metal (so called because its shape is round, like the pastry called a chararah - Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 11:3).
and from the tire of a wheel. The metal covering made for wagon wheels.
the plates. Thin sheets of metal.
and from the coverings. The covering of a vessel that was removed (and any covering of a vessel is not susceptible to impurity while it is attached, above 4:4).
and from the bases of vessels. The bottoms of vessels.
and from the necks of vessels. The necks of vessels.
and from the handles of vessels. The grips of vessels.
and from the shocholet. Excess protrusions that were cut off the vessel in the course of making it.
and from the gerodet. Metal crumbs that were scraped or filed off the vessel.

these are pure, because all of these are unfinished metal vessels. Either they were made of inferior materials that are not worked and finished, such as the esht and the chararah, or they were formed by joining pieces of metal, such as the coverings and the plates, so their form is not perfect and they are considered unfinished vessels (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 11:3; Arukh HaShulchan 197:13; see other explanations in Kesef Mishneh and in Rambam LeAm).
these are susceptible to impurity because they are not unfinished. Since they were made of material that was part of a finished vessel and was properly worked.

but nails of which it is not known, etc.. Apparently, because of the small size of the nails, one cannot tell whether they were made from vessels and are susceptible to impurity, or were made from the esht and are not susceptible to impurity.
they are pure. For most nails are not made from vessels (Arukh HaShulchan, ibid.).
and even if he prepared them for a vessel. For example, he prepared them to serve as a needle or a skewer (for an ordinary nail is not a vessel until he prepares it for that purpose, as below 10:1).
a needle that he did not pierce. He did not make a hole in it, and it cannot be used for sewing.
he filed it and prepared it for that from the start. If, when he filed the needle, he intended not to pierce it.
is susceptible to impurity, since a thorn is removed with it. It is fit for use and its work is finished.

but if he is going to pierce it, it is like other unfinished metal vessels and is not susceptible to impurity. Although it is fit for removing a thorn, its work is not yet finished, since he intended it for sewing and it is not yet ready for that.
and unfinished wooden vessels are impure. Above 5:1.

and plain metal vessels are impure, and plain wooden vessels are pure, by Torah law. Above 1:9-10. It was explained there that, by rabbinic law, some plain wooden articles are susceptible to impurity.
thus what is impure among wooden vessels is pure among metal vessels. Unfinished vessels are impure when made of wood and pure when made of metal.
and what is impure among metal vessels is pure among wooden vessels. Plain vessels without a receptacle are impure if made of metal and pure if made of wood.
the sword. A sword.
and the spear. A lance.
and the helmet. Made of metal to protect the head.
and the greaves. Which have metal parts to protect the shins.
the katlah. A small chain made of metal links, or a thread on which beads of precious stones or precious metals are strung.
and the nezamim. An ornament hung from the nose or the ears (earrings).
whether or not they have a seal on them. For they used to engrave letters or shapes on the ring and use it to seal documents.
even a dinar that was disqualified. A coin that is not used as money.
and he prepared it to hang on a little girl's neck, is susceptible to impurity. Because it became an ornament. But an ordinary coin is not a vessel (and see also below 9:10).
and for the handles of vessels. A ring attached to the handle of a vessel, for decoration or for the vessel's use (Tiferet Yisrael, Kelim 12:1).
and they are not susceptible to impurity on their own. When they are not part of another vessel that is susceptible to impurity.

except for an animal's bell and those that make a sound for people. A bell hung on an animal, or on vessels meant to make a sound for people, for example so that one knows where the animal is (Tosafot, Shabbat 58b), or to make a sound when the vessel is moved.
zugin. Bells without a clapper that do not make a sound.
for a mortar and for a cradle... are pure. For they have the law of ornaments of vessels.
if he made clappers for them. And they make a sound.

they are susceptible to impurity, since they were made to make a sound for people. For example, so that a child will fall asleep in the cradle to the sound of the bells (Rashi, Shabbat 58b), or so that people will hear the bells hung on a Torah scroll and rise in its honor (Chasdei David, Kelim, Bava Metzia 1:13).

and even if their clappers were removed, they are susceptible to impurity, since it is fit to strike it against a potsherd. A sound can be made by striking the bell against a potsherd. Although originally it is not susceptible to impurity when it has no clapper, since he made a clapper for it and it became fit to be susceptible to impurity, it is still susceptible as long as it can serve for something similar to its original task (compare above 6:8).
if it was made for a child, it is susceptible to impurity only through its clapper, for it was made for sound. So that the child will play with it and it will make a sound.
and if it was made for an adult, it is an ornament. For some people hang a bell on their necks as an ornament (Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 58a).
masks. Masks.
and all seals are pure. If they are made of wood or coral (Chasdei David, Kelim, Bava Metzia 1:11).
and all rings are pure except a finger ring. Which is an ornament for a person.

but a ring with which he girds his loins or which he fastens between his shoulders is pure. One that serves as a buckle for a belt or with which he fastens the sleeves; these rings serve vessels and not the person.
the ring of the animal's chain. A ring attached to the band placed around the animal's neck; a person inserts his finger into it to pull or lead the animal.
become eligible for impurity. They become fit to be susceptible to impurity.
by intention. Only the owner's intention is effective, not the intention of another (below 25:11).
they leave the status of impurity. They become vessels that are not susceptible to impurity, and if they were impure before, they become pure.
an animal's ring or a vessel's ring that he intended to make into a person's ring. To change its purpose and use it as an ornament.
it is susceptible to impurity by this intention. It becomes fit to be susceptible to impurity from now on.
if the ring was for a person. Made as an ornament.
a deaf-mute, an imbecile, and a minor have action but have no intention, as we explained regarding the preparation of foods. Hilchot Tumat Ochlin 13:4, 14:2 (and see also above 2:1).
a door bell. A sound-making bell fixed to the door of the house, which is not susceptible to impurity because from the start it was made to be attached to the ground (see below 9:1).
and that of an animal. Which is susceptible to impurity from the start (above 5:7).

even if he attached it to the ground... it is susceptible to impurity as it was, until he changes it by an action to its body. Fixing the bell to the door does not change anything in it, since it serves to make a sound both before it was fixed and after it was fixed.
a craftsman who makes and sets aside bells for doors and for animals. Who makes bells suitable for both doors and animals, and the buyer uses them for whatever he needs.
one for lying. Which is susceptible to impurity.
and one for tents. Which is not susceptible to impurity.
one for forms. On which figures are drawn to serve as a model for the embroiderer to embroider like them; it is not susceptible to impurity because it is not considered a garment.
and one for tents. To make a curtain or screen from it; sometimes people wrap themselves in it and it is considered a garment and is susceptible to impurity (Babylonian Talmud, Beitzah 14b).
all metal vessels that have a name of their own. Even though they are part of another vessel, they have a separate name that is specific to them.
and the bolt. A bar.
and the socket beneath the hinge. A cup-shaped vessel sunk into the ground into which the door's pivot is inserted.
and the beam. A metal house beam that serves the door.
and the spout. A gutter.
because these are made for the ground. To be attached to the ground, such as the socket and the spout.
or to serve the wood. Such as the bolt, which is not attached to the ground but serves the door, which is made of wood.
are not susceptible to impurity, even before they are fixed. For anything attached to the ground is like the ground and is pure, and metal that serves wood is pure (above 4:5).
and any metal vessel that has a qualified name. That is not called by an independent name but only as part of another vessel.
is not susceptible to impurity on its own. When it is not attached to the other parts of the vessel.

the scorpion of a harness is impure. A harness is an animal's gear, and the scorpion is the metal part that attaches to the harness and goes into the animal's mouth. It is impure because it is called simply "scorpion" without a qualifying name.

and its cheekpieces, on the animal's cheeks on either side, are pure. The irons placed on the animal's cheeks are pure because they have a qualified name: they are called "cheekpieces of a harness" and not simply "cheekpieces."

and when they are joined, everything is susceptible to impurity. When the cheekpieces are attached to the other parts of the bridle, all the parts are susceptible to impurity if impurity touched any one of them.
iron plates... are not susceptible to impurity because they have no name of their own. Because they are part of an iron helmet and are not called simply "plates."
and if they have a water receptacle, they are susceptible to impurity like any receptacle. For a receptacle is susceptible to impurity even if it has no name of its own (Arukh HaShulchan 199:6).
an earring made like a pot below and like a lentil above. Its lower part is made as a receptacle and its upper part is made like a metal lentil.
and its tzenirah. The thin part of the earring that goes into the ear or the nose.
if the earring was made like a cluster. It has many gold grains joined to one another in the shape of a cluster.
one ring that girls place on one foot. On each foot separately.

which has no shape of an ornament but is like a vessel's ring or a ring with which one fastens between his shoulders. The purpose of the garter is to hold up the stockings so they do not fall, so it is not considered a person's ornament but like a vessel's ring, which is pure (see above 8:7, 8:9).
but two rings that girls put on their legs, with a chain hanging between them from one to the other. So that they will not take long strides (Commentary to the Mishnah, Shabbat 6:4).
are susceptible to impurity because they are among the ornaments of girls. For when the garters are connected, they are meant for the direct use of the person.
a necklace whose links are of metal and are on a thread of wool or flax. A chain made of perforated beads of gold or silver strung on a thread.

if its thread was of metal... and the links broke and the thread remained, it is susceptible to impurity on its own. The metal thread is impure as an ornament when it is whole. The stones or glass are not susceptible to impurity, for the impurity of ornaments applies only to metal vessels.

the remnants of a necklace, enough to go around a little girl's neck. If a necklace made of links of precious stones and a metal thread was cut, and what remains of it is long enough to go around the neck of a little girl, it is susceptible to impurity.
all metal lids. Covers made of metal.
except the lid of a heater. Which they used to turn over and use as a receptacle.
and the lid of a physicians' basket. A vessel in the shape of a basket.
because they place the bandage in it. The physician places the bandages in it.
a metal lid that he filed and polished and made into a mirror is susceptible to impurity. The polishing makes the lid a vessel in its own right.
all metal weights are susceptible to impurity. They are a vessel that serves a person.
the beam of a wooden balance on which iron hooks hang. A weight hangs from one end of the beam, and the goods to be weighed are hung from the other end.
is susceptible to impurity because of the hooks hanging from it. It has the status of wood that serves metal (above 4:5).

this applies to the balances of flax sellers and wool sellers. The weight always hangs on the beam. Therefore even if it is not fixed to it they are considered one vessel, and the beam is susceptible to impurity (Arukh HaShulchan 200:6).

but that of householders is not susceptible to impurity. Householders' weights do not hang on the beam permanently, so the beam is not considered one vessel with the weight and is pure, like plain wooden vessels.
until the hooks are fixed to it. He attached them with a permanent attachment; then they have the law of one vessel in which the wood serves the metal (ibid.).
weights that broke, even though he put them back and weighs with them. He places the pieces of the weight together in the pan of the scale and thus gets the same weight as the whole weight.
are not susceptible to impurity. Each fragment on its own is not fit for weighing, and so it is not a vessel (Chasdei David, Kelim, Bava Metzia 2:16).

if he set aside from them half-litras, third-litras, or quarter-ritls, they are susceptible to impurity. If a fragment serves on its own as a weight for a smaller measure, it has the law of an ordinary weight and is susceptible to impurity.
a sela that was disqualified. A coin that is not used as money, either because the government forbade its use or because it was worn down and lost weight.

the porters' hook is pure. A wooden staff to which a large iron hook is attached; the porter hooks it behind the load on his shoulder and holds the end of the staff in his hand, using it to help hold the load (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 12:2).
and that of peddlers is susceptible to impurity. Peddlers carry by means of hooks bowls of spices and the like, and they are susceptible to impurity by virtue of the bowls (Tiferet Yisrael, ibid.).

the hook of the bedposts is pure. Hooks hung on the bedposts, which are rods standing at the head and foot of the bed, on which a canopy is hung. They are pure because the bedposts are plain wooden articles.

and that of a step-stool is susceptible to impurity. A step-stool (dargash) is a kind of low stool that serves as a step for climbing onto the large bed. Its hooks are used for holding when climbing onto the bed (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 12:2).
the hook of the fishermen's net with which they catch fish is pure. Hooks hung on a fishermen's net, which is a vessel that is not susceptible to impurity (above 5:10).
and that of a chest is susceptible to impurity. Like the chest itself, which is susceptible to impurity when it does not hold forty se'ah (see above 3:2).
the hook of a wooden lampstand is pure. Like the lampstand (above 4:1).
and that of a table is susceptible to impurity. Like the table (ibid.).
the metal hook belonging to it. The hook hanging from it.
and its chain. A chain attached to the vessel.
each one on its own. The hook or the chain that are not attached to another vessel.
and even a hook on the walls. That is not part of another vessel.
a chain that has a lock. That has a padlock.
is susceptible to impurity. For it is considered a vessel.
and one made for tying. To tie a person, animals, or objects.

is pure. Because it has no lock, it is not designated for a particular task but is used for various tasks each time; therefore it has the law of a rope and is not considered a vessel in its own right (Chazon Ish, Kelim 15:1).
a chain of wholesale merchants. Merchants who sell grain in large quantities.
a chain of land surveyors. Who measure the area of land.
and their pegs that they drive into the ground when they survey. To mark the point the chain reached.
are susceptible to impurity. For they serve people.
and a chain of wood gatherers. With which they tie bundles of wood.
the chain of a large bucket. Attached to a large bucket.

four handbreadths of it next to the bucket become impure with the bucket, because it is needed for the bucket. Because of the weight of the bucket, people hold only the four handbreadths next to the bucket, and these are considered a handle of the vessel.
and the rest is pure, since it has no name of its own. This part is not a handle of the vessel and also has no name of its own, and so it is not considered a vessel.
and the chain of a small bucket, ten handbreadths. The small bucket is lighter, so one can pull it from a greater distance.
the metal ball. Which is among the implements of war or of play (Chasdei David, Kelim, Bava Metzia 2:15).
and the builder's crowbar. A metal rod used for prying up stones and rolling loads (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 14:3, according to Rabbi Yosef Kapach there).
and the carpenter's chisel. An iron rod with a wooden handle used by the carpenter for carving wood.
and the smith's anvil. An iron beam; the smith sits at one side of it and strikes the vessel on the other side.

and the plumb bob and the builder's weight. A weight hung on a cord and used to make sure the wall is built straight (the plumb bob and the weight are different models of the same tool - Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 12:8).
and the iron beaters with which they beat olives. Iron rods used to heap the olives onto the millstones in the olive press (ibid.).
and the metal hopper. A funnel into which grains of wheat are put and from which they pour into the millstones for grinding.
and the knife with which scribes cut the tip of a reed pen. So that the reed will be sharp and comfortable for writing.
and the metal pen. A writing reed.
and the ken and the kanah with which scribes rule lines. The ken is the reed with which lines are drawn on the parchment, and the kanah is the ruler used for this purpose.

nails with which the ceiling is strengthened... are not susceptible to impurity. They are meant to be part of a building or of another vessel, and are not considered vessels with a separate use or a name of their own (see Noda BiYehudah, second edition, Yoreh De'ah 137).
and likewise nails driven into walls to hang things on. To hang clothes or vessels on them.
a nail that he prepared to open and lock with. That is, he bent the nail or sharpened it and made it into a key.
or that he put into a hand mill. To serve as a pivot connecting the parts of the mill (Hechatzer U'Matkanehah, chapter 2).
or a donkey mill. A mill that is turned by a donkey.
he prepared it to open a barrel with. To use it to pierce the barrel (Rav Shimshon, Kelim 12:5).

is pure until he refines it. Until he sharpens the tip of the nail so that it is ready to pierce the barrel (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 12:5). Some explain that he must refine the nail with fire, because the nail must be stronger than an ordinary nail in order to open the barrel (Rav Shimshon there; Ra'avad).
a nail made as a marker to guard the entrance. One places the nail on the door, and if the nail moves from its place it is known that someone opened the door.
is not susceptible to impurity. Because this nail serves only as a marker and its substance is not used, so it is not considered a utensil.
likewise the nail of a money-changer's table, on which he hangs the scales and the purse. A money changer; the nail is fixed in his table.
likewise the hangers of the scrapers. Nails fixed in the walls of the bathhouse, on which metal tools are hung for scraping the legs of the bathers.

even though these nails differ in shape from other nails for fixing. Even though these nails have a special shape, different from ordinary nails made for fixing into a wall, they are not considered utensils in their own right.
and the nail of a sundial. The nail of a sundial that casts a shadow.

the weaver's nail etc.. To ease passing the weft threads between the stretched warp threads, they would wind the weft thread on a bobbin, a device made of a metal nail fixed inside a wooden tube, which was passed between the warp threads (this device is called 'imah' below, 20:16, and is not the 'imah' mentioned below in halachah 14).
a metal yoke. The pole attached to a wagon and laid lengthwise between the two animals that pull the wagon.
and the katrev. The pole laid across the necks of the animals.
and the wings that receive the straps. Pieces of iron protruding from the katrev, to which are attached the straps that tie the katrev to the animal's neck.
and the iron beneath the animals' necks. Pieces of iron tied on the animal's neck so that it will not be choked by the straps that tie the katrev.
and the support. An iron peg at the front of the wagon on which it rests when it is not harnessed to animals.

and the machger. A peg at the end of the yoke whose function is to stabilize the wagon (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 14:4). It may be projections extending sideways from the end of the yoke near where it is attached to the wagon, which limit the yoke's ability to rotate on its axis (Tavnit Kelim there).
and the receptacles. Vessels in which the load carried on the wagon is placed.
and the bell. A bell.
and the hook. A hook used to tie down the goods on the wagon.

and the nail that joins all of them. Each of the aforementioned parts of the wagon (the explanation follows the Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 14:4; other commentators identified the parts of the wagon differently).
a wooden yoke that is plated. With metal, for all plated utensils are pure (above 4:4).
and wings made for decoration. The ends of the katrev to which no straps are attached but which were made for beauty.
and the tubes that produce sound. Thin pipes that rattle and make a sound when the wagon travels.
and the lead at the side of the animals' necks. The lead at the side of the neck, which has no use in the wagon.
and the rim of a wheel. The metal hoop around the wheel.
and the plates and the platings. Thin sheets of metal.
and all the other nails in it. That do not connect the parts that are susceptible to impurity.
all of these are pure. Because they are not considered utensils in their own right.
the olive press's scorpion. An iron at the end of the beam of the olive press, with which the olives are crushed.

a cabinet of ground-bean sellers. A wooden cabinet of sellers of ground beans, built carelessly and not considered a utensil (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 12:4). Some explain that such a cabinet is not movable and is pure because it is a wooden vessel made to stay in place (Rash there).

if there was a metal wagon beneath it, it is susceptible to impurity. By virtue of being a metal utensil, and it is not secondary to the cabinet. Some explain that the cabinet too is impure because it is attached to the wagon (Chazon Ish, Kelim 15:7).

a pepper mill. The mill is made of three parts. In the upper part the peppers are ground, and it is impure as a metal utensil. In the middle part there is a sieve through which the ground pepper falls below while the coarse pieces remain on it, and it is impure as a sieve. In the lower part there is a bowl into which the fine pepper falls, and it is impure as a receptacle. All these parts are connected to one another, yet even when separated each one is susceptible to impurity and is considered a utensil in its own right and not a broken utensil (Commentary to the Mishnah, Beitzah 2:9).

the metal door of a householders' tower is not susceptible to impurity. The door of a wooden cabinet is not susceptible to impurity because it has no name of its own, or because the tower is a utensil made to stay in place (above 3:2), which is not susceptible to impurity, and the door is nullified in relation to it.
the bandage. A bandage.
metal plates with which one shakes the pot. Tongs with which one grips the hot pot.

and those fixed in the stove are pure. Iron supports attached to the stove on which the pot is placed so that it will not sit directly on the fire and burn. They are pure because they are attached to the ground.
the tongs with which he presses the wick. With which he trims the head of the wick that has turned to charcoal and does not burn well.

and the tubes that hold the millstones from above. In some types of mills there were two large holes in the upper stone, into which thick wooden poles were inserted to turn the mill. To fix the poles in the holes, nails were driven into the poles through small holes in the stone (Tarbut Chomrit, vol. 1, p. 144).
a clostra with which doors are locked. A bolt whose head is thickened like a ball.
if it was of metal, it is susceptible to impurity. Because it is a utensil in its own right.
if it was of wood and plated with metal, it is pure. For all plated utensils are pure (above 4:4).
the pin and the purna. The pin is the tongue of the lock that enters the purna, a sort of box, when the door is closed.
impure. Because each one is considered a utensil in its own right.
a metal whorl. A hemispherical piece of metal attached to a spindle to stabilize it and add weight to it during spinning.
the spindle. Part of the distaff-spindle, a wooden rod on which the spun thread is wound after being twirled.
and the imah. The stick on which is placed the raw wool or flax from which threads are spun on the spindle.
and the staff. A metal one, with which one drives the animal (Rash, Kelim 11:6).
and the symphonia. A sophisticated flute that has a mouthpiece for blowing and various parts that assist in playing.
if it had a receptacle, wings. Parts extending from it and used for playing.
even though it is plated, it is impure. Because the place of the wings cannot be plated (Commentary to the Mishnah there).
the trumpet. A trumpet.
that is divided into sections. Built of parts that can be taken apart and reassembled, and each part by itself is not considered a utensil.
if only an expert knows how to restore it, it is susceptible to impurity when assembled. For then the connection is strong and it is considered a utensil.
but if anyone can take it apart and restore it, it is not susceptible to impurity. Because the connection is weak and the parts are not considered one utensil (Kesef Mishneh).
the end on which one places the mouth when blowing is susceptible to impurity by itself. It is susceptible to impurity when taken apart, since a sound can be produced with it.
and the other, wide end is not susceptible to impurity by itself. Since a sound cannot be produced with it when it is separate from the mouthpiece of the instrument.
and when connected, all of it is impure. For all of it is considered one utensil.
the stems of a lamp. A lamp composed of parts: the base of the lamp, stems extending from it, and a round platform on which the lamp is placed, called a flower.
its flower and its base become impure by themselves. Because they have a name of their own, or because they have a receptacle (Tiferet Yisrael, Kelim 11:7).
is susceptible to impurity. Because it has the form of a utensil or because it is not fixed in the ground.
a saw. A saw.

who made its teeth into the hole of the door. He wants to make the hole in the door smaller and fixes the saw there to serve as a grating (it may be the hole through which the key is inserted; see the explanation below 11:18).
even though he uses it. That he also uses it for sawing, by moving wood back and forth over the teeth fixed in the door.
it is not susceptible to impurity. For it no longer serves for work in its usual way.

and if after it became impure he put it into the hole of the door, it remains in its impurity until he fixes it with a nail. For to become pure of impurity, a change in the manner of its work is not enough to nullify it; he must fix it with a nail, which shows more clearly that he has nullified its status as a utensil.

if he turned it upward, downward, or sideways, it is pure. He fixed it flush against the sides of the hole so that the teeth do not protrude toward the opening of the hole. Since the saw is inverted and cannot be used for sawing, it is completely nullified from its function and pure (and see Chazon Ish, Bava Metzia 4:10, who explains differently by comparison to below 11:24).

an arrow beam, which is a target that has metal tongues. A wooden beam serving as a target at which arrows are shot, with pieces of metal attached to the beam that one tries to hit precisely (Aruch HaShulchan 202:18).
is susceptible to impurity. Since it has the law of a wooden utensil that serves the metal.

and one placed on the feet of prisoners is pure. A metal stock in which the feet of prisoners are locked is pure because it is not a utensil (Rosh, Kelim 12:1) or because it is fixed in the ground (Tiferet Yisrael there).
and the collar. A ring and chain on the necks of prisoners.
all according to what it is. According to the special use of the utensil.
as long as the utensil can do work similar to its work. Work similar to the work for which it was intended before it broke.
a metal bucket that broke but can still be filled with. Water in a drinking quantity (Tosefta, Kelim Bava Metzia 4:1).
a kettle, to heat water in it. So that he can heat drinking water in it.
the heater. A vessel for heating water, larger than a kettle.

to hold sela coins. To place in it sela coins, which are large and will not fall through the hole. Apparently they would use the heater for this purpose too when it was whole, and therefore it is considered as doing work similar to its original work (Tiferet Yisrael, Kelim 14:1, Chazon Ish, Kelim 18:1). Or, because metal utensils were expensive, people were accustomed to use them for another purpose once they were punctured (Chazon Ish there).
the lapas. A large metal vessel.
to hold metal cups. So that cups can be placed in it.
to hold perutot. Perutah coins, which are small, and apparently they would use cups for this even when whole.

wine measures, to measure wine with them. So that it does not run out through the hole. Some explain that if the wine drips slowly, in a way that does not interfere with measuring, the utensil is still impure (Tiferet Yisrael, Kelim 14:1).
and oil measures, to measure oil with them. Since it is thick and comes out through a larger hole.
a mustard strainer. They would soak the mustard in water and then strain it through a metal strainer.
in which three holes were broken through at the bottom, one into the other. Three adjacent holes were torn, creating one large hole.
pure, because it does not serve for work similar to its work. Because the mustard falls through the hole.
a rake whose blade was removed, even though it is like a hammer. Since one can use the iron at the head of its handle as a hammer.
a wool comb. Made of wood with teeth of metal.
if three remain in one place, it is impure. Since one can still comb wool with it.

if the outer one was one of the three, it is pure. The outer teeth of the comb are larger and thicker than the other teeth and one cannot comb with them. Therefore the outer tooth is not counted among the teeth.
because one cannot comb flax with it. Some wrote that the word "flax" should be deleted, since this concerns a wool comb (Meir Ayin, Kelim). Others explained in other ways (see Mirkevet HaMishneh).

two were removed from the comb and he made them into a tweezer, they are impure. Two teeth were removed from the comb and he made of them a small tongs with which hairs are plucked from the body; they become susceptible to impurity from now on as a new utensil.
and prepared it for a lamp. To remove the wicks from the lamp.

and if the tooth was thick and large, even though he did not prepare it, it is susceptible to impurity by itself. For one engraves with it on a wax tablet (Tosefta, Kelim Bava Metzia 3:15, below halachah 14).
a flax comb. With which flax fibers are combed, and its teeth are larger than those of a wool comb.

the broken kedumim. A device used to retrieve buckets that fell into a well, made of an iron hoop from which hang short metal chains, at the end of each of which is a hook on which the buckets are hung (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 13:7; some explain in other ways, see the Commentary of the Geonim and Rash there).
and their hooks remain intact. The hooks and the chains.
a saw. A saw.
from which every second tooth was removed. Every other tooth, so that no two consecutive teeth remain.

a full sit remains in one place. Whole consecutive teeth remain to the extent of a full sit, which is the width of two fingers, that is, half a handbreadth (see Commentary to the Mishnah, Orlah 3:2 and the note of Rabbi Yosef Kafih there, Commentary to the Mishnah, Shabbat 13:4 and the notes of Rabbi Y. Shilat there; this measure differs from the 'width of a sit,' which is about two handbreadths - see Hilchot Shabbat 9:7).
impure, since one can saw with what remains. To saw with the teeth that remain.
the adze. An axe, a tool for cutting and uprooting trees (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 13:4).
and the chisel. A kind of narrow knife for scraping, engraving and carving.
and the carving tool. A tool for carving wood (Commentary of the Geonim, Kelim 13:4).
and the drill. A tool for making holes in wood.
that were nicked. Small breaks were made in them.
are still susceptible to impurity. Since they can still be used.
the tip. The end of the tool, made of hard iron.
pure. Since they are no longer fit for work.
and all of them that were split in two are impure. Since one can still cut and sharpen with them.
and the runki. A tool for smoothing wood, made of a wooden handle in which iron is set (Commentary of the Geonim there). [Note: in some manuscripts the reading is 'the dunki'.]
by itself. Since the iron is separate from the handle.
the sword. A sword.
and the curved knife like a sickle. Of a rounded shape.
and the spear. A spear.
and a hand sickle. A small rounded knife for household use.
and a harvest sickle. A sickle for reaping grain.
a coat of mail that was split lengthwise. Its right side and left side were separated.
pure. Since it protects only half the body and is not fit for its function.
widthwise. Its upper and lower parts were separated.
if it serves its original function, it is impure. If it can be worn in a way that protects part of the body.
it wore out and most of it remains: if the upper part, it is impure. Because it can be worn and the shoulders hold it up (like the law of a robe below 22:16).
and if the lower part, it is pure. Since it cannot be held on the body and worn, and it is like a broken utensil.
he cut off a piece of it and made a link for jewelry, it is susceptible to impurity. Since it is considered a new utensil and is susceptible to impurity by the law of jewelry.
a goldsmiths' tube. A pipe through which smiths blow air to fan the coals and melt gold.
and the glaziers'. Who melt glass.
and the blacksmiths'. Who heat iron.
and the glassblowers'. Who blow into a ball of glowing glass and thereby form a vessel.
that was split lengthwise is pure. Since one cannot blow through it.
widthwise, if it serves its original function. If enough of its length remained for that.
tongs. Pincers, tongs.
of barbers. With which hair is plucked.
and of physicians. Who use it for surgical needs.
and of glassblowers. With which they hold the glowing lump of glass when making a vessel from it.
that became dull. That does not shine.
a needle whose pierced end was removed. The end with the hole through which the thread is passed.
or its point. The pointed end.

and if he prepared it to wind thread around it for embroidering, it is impure. To wind thread around it so that it is more convenient to embroider with it, for this use requires neither the hole of the needle nor its point, and it is like a new utensil and impure.
but a sack needle. Of sack sewers, which is large and thick.
whose pierced end was removed. And one can no longer sew with it.
impure. Even if he did not prepare it for this.

because it makes a mark with the other end. With the pointed end, since people are accustomed to use it for engraving on a wax tablet even when it is whole, and it was not nullified from all its original function (Mishnah Acharonah, Kelim 13:5).
the needle around which one winds the crimson or the gold. Around which crimson or gold threads are wound.
whose work is not sewing. That was intended from the outset for winding.
if it prevents sewing. If the rust makes it impossible to use the needle for sewing.
he filed them and sharpened them, they return to their former impurity. Like the law of fragments of metal utensils from which he made new utensils (below 12:1).
and likewise a tzinorah. A needle without a hole or point, with a hook-like curve at its end, used to clean the burnt wick from a lamp.
that he straightened. He straightened it.

a key bent like an arkubah. Whose handle has an angle like a knee (the lock in their day was on the inner side of the door, and to open the door from outside they would insert a hand through a hole in the door and push the teeth of the key into the bolt. The teeth would move the spring that holds the bolt, and then the bolt could be pulled with the key. Bending the key was needed to allow a person standing outside the door to grip and pull the bolt - see Tarbut Chomrit, vol. 1, p. 49).
that broke from its arkubah is pure. If it broke below the angle it is pure, since one cannot open with it from outside.

and likewise a key made in the shape of a gam. In the shape of the Greek letter gamma, which looks like this: Γ. That is, the key has no arkubah, only a line with a projection at its end, similar to simple keys today.
that broke at its gam. At the point where the key bends.
if it had teeth and holes etc.. That at the end of the key there are projections and holes that enter the lock and open it.
impure, since it is still a key. For even when broken it still has the shape of a key.
if the teeth were removed, it is impure because of the holes etc.. For it still has the shape of a key.
or if the holes were broken through one into the other. And became one hole.
to lift the ashes with it. The ashes in the oven.
whose bowl was removed. Was removed from it.
impure because of its teeth. For one can still use it as a fork, and likewise if its teeth were removed one can use it as a spoon.
and likewise a kohl applicator whose bowl was removed, with which the kohl is scooped. A tool for painting the eye with a small spoon at its end for scooping the paint.
impure because of the rod with which the eye is painted. Since one can use the other end of the tool, which is pointed and with which the eye is painted.
a spoon like a lattice. Made like a net.
and likewise a metal pen with which one writes with one end. By engraving in wax or by dipping in ink and drawing on parchment.
and erases with the other end. Since its other end is wider and with it one smooths the wax in which letters were engraved, or it is sharp and with it one scrapes the letters from the parchment.
so that it reaches the joints of his fingers. To the place where the fingers join the palm.
if a full hand-width of its length remains. A length equal to the width of the palm.
an axe. A carpenters' tool that has two sides.
and this is the side with which the carpenter planes. He carves wood with it, and it is made like a hammer whose end is wide and flat.
its splitting part. The sharp, rounded side used for splitting wood.
its socket. The hole of the axe into which the wooden handle is inserted.
pure. Since one cannot strike with an axe without the handle.
a plow-scraper that was nicked. A wide chisel used to remove earth stuck to the plow and to clear roots that obstruct the plow, a part of whose edge was removed.
its socket. The hole into which one inserts the wood that serves as the handle of the plow-scraper.

the ox-goad, which is the teacher etc.. This halachah explains what the plow-scraper mentioned in the previous halachah is, as well as the other parts of the ox-goad that will be mentioned below (20:12, 28:4).
and this iron is called a darban. With which one pricks the animal to urge it on and direct it.
a metal nursing tube, which is like a tube that became impure. A small metal pipe used as a straw for drinking from a barrel or for other uses.
after he fixes it on a stick. At the head of the stick, for decoration.
or on a door. At the bottom of the door, so that it will not rot from the moisture in the ground.
and connects it with the wood, it becomes pure. Since it was nullified from its former use, it is purified of its impurity.

it did not become impure, and he fixed it on a stick or on a door, it is susceptible to impurity in its place. For fixing does not nullify the nursing tube from being a utensil, but only makes it like a new utensil that is susceptible to impurity from now on (Kesef Mishneh, Chazon Ish, Kelim Bava Metzia 4:10). Some explain that there is no distinction between becoming pure of old impurity and becoming susceptible to future impurity, rather a nursing tube that he joined to the wood and fixed with nails became completely pure, but if he merely fixed the tube and did not join it to the wood with nails, so that it can be taken out and used, the tube did not become pure (Aruch HaShulchan 204:17, Chazon Ish, Kelim 18:11, and see Sidrei Taharot, Kelim 136:2).
a metal baker's board. A metal board on which the baker arranges the dough.
that he fixed in the wall is impure. Since one can still place dough on it.

he melted them and made other utensils from them, they return to their former impurity. If he melted the fragments and made a new utensil from them, it is impure with the same impurity with which the first utensil was impure before it broke.

metal utensils have no complete purity until one immerses them in a mikveh while whole. But if one immersed the fragments and made a utensil from them, the immersion is of no use, and if he made a utensil from them it returns to its former impurity.

a decree lest his utensil become impure etc.. The Sages feared that people would equate the law of a melted utensil with that of an immersed utensil, and say that just as a utensil that broke and was melted is completely pure immediately, so a utensil that was immersed is completely pure immediately after its immersion. But that is not the law: a utensil that has immersed from its impurity is not completely pure and still disqualifies terumah until evening comes after its immersion (Hilchot Shear Avot HaTumot 10:1, Hilchot Terumot 7:2). They decreed specifically for metal utensils, which can be joined by melting so that no sign remains that they broke. But for other utensils they did not decree, since when they are repaired it is evident that they broke, because one must join them with nails or new sewing and the like, and therefore they did not fear that people would purify them by breaking and joining them (see Rash, Kelim 2:1).
became impure through a corpse. And one must sprinkle purification water on it on the third and seventh days of its impurity and afterward immerse it (Hilchot Parah 11:1).
and a sprinkling before melting does not combine with a sprinkling after melting. The sprinkling on the old utensil does not combine with the sprinkling on the new utensil.
impure iron that he mixed with pure iron. He melted iron from a utensil that became impure together with pure iron and made a utensil from them.
and if the majority is of dung, it is not susceptible to impurity. Like the law of dung utensils, which are not susceptible to impurity (above 1:6).
pure metal utensils that were coated with impure tin are impure. Utensils that were worn down and he coated them with impure metal that he melted, to renew them.
impure. Because the coating is not something separate from the utensil but its essence, since without the coating the utensil is not fit for use, so the law of the utensil is the law of the coating.
but one who makes utensils from impure tin. Who scraped the coating from the utensil and made a new utensil from it.
they are pure. Since this is not common, the Sages did not decree concerning it (Chok Natan, Tas'ar Kelim p. 32).
an axe that he made from pure iron and made its ushap from impure. An axe has two sides, one used for splitting wood and the other for carving and carpentry, called the ushap (above 11:21).
it is impure. Since the main function of the utensil is carving wood and not splitting.
a pure axe that he tipped with impure iron. He plated its edge with hardened iron, and that iron was impure.

pure. For we follow the main body of the utensil, since the blow of the axe is based on the force generated by the axe's weight and it can be used without tipping; but in utensils whose function depends on having a sharp edge we follow the tipping (above 11:7, Chazon Ish, Kelim Bava Metzia 1:3).
a cup. A cup.
and its base. The bottom of the vessel.
everything follows the part that receives and does the work. The base is the main part of a cup because it makes it a receptacle.
for example, one that became impure through idolatry. See Hilchot Shear Avot HaTumot 6:1.
because their impurity is essentially rabbinic, as we explained. Above 1:5.

they did not decree for them regarding old impurity. They are not like metal utensils that became impure with rabbinic impurity, concerning which there is a doubt whether they return to their former impurity or not (as explained in the previous halachah).
