For metal utensils can become impure by Torah law, whereas glass utensils are not susceptible to impurity at all by Torah law, and the Sages did not decree concerning them at all (Tosafot, Shabbat 16a).

are not susceptible to impurity because they are unlike earthenware. For fragments of earthenware vessels are susceptible to impurity if they are fit to receive (below 18:10). But fragments of glass vessels are not susceptible to impurity because they cut the hands and one does not use them.

the base is not susceptible to impurity even though it is like a bowl. Even though the bottom of the vessel is shaped like a small inverted bowl, and when the vessel breaks one can turn the base over and use it (see Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 30:1).
and if he trimmed the place of the break and polished it with a file. He smoothed and sanded the place of the break.
it is susceptible to impurity. Since one can use it without being cut.
a small flask. A jar with a narrow neck.
whose mouth was removed. Its neck was broken.
because one does not put the hand into it but pours from it. And so does not touch the sharp place of the break.
but a large one carried with two hands whose mouth was removed is pure. For from a large vessel one does not pour but takes what is inside with the hands, and they might get scratched.
paliton. Perfume.
because it wounds his finger when he takes the perfume out of it. For one does not pour the perfume but takes a small amount of it with the finger.
large jars. Large jugs.

because he prepares them for pickling. To pickle food in them in vinegar or wine. Even though the vessel is sharp and might injure, it is customary to use it so, since the pickled items are put in once and taken out after a long time, not frequently.
a cup most of whose rim is chipped. The rim of the cup is slightly broken and is not smooth around most of the circumference of the rim.
pure. Since the chip cuts the lips and one cannot drink from it.
a third of its circumference was chipped, for most of its height. A third of the wall of the cup broke, and at the place of the break less than half its height remains.
with tin. Tin.

pure. For they were lenient with glass utensils, whose impurity is rabbinic (Sidrei Taharot, Kelim 264:2). Some explain that in glass the plug falls out easily and therefore is not considered a plug (Aruch HaShulchan 206:14, and see Chazon Ish, Kelim Bava Batra 7:9).
and a cup or flask that was punctured, whether above or below, are pure. Since the liquids run out through the hole and one cannot drink or pour from them.
the serving bowl. A large bowl for serving food.
from above, they are impure. Since one can still use the intact part and put liquids in it.
if they can receive hot as cold, they are impure. If one can put hot water in them and the crack will not widen and cause the vessel to burst.
and if not, they are pure. Since their use is to serve hot food in them, and if they are not fit for that they are nullified from their function.
the cut cups. Whose rims were cut in their manufacture and not smoothed.
even though their rims scrape the mouth. They scratch the mouth a bit when one drinks from them.
are susceptible to impurity. Because they were made so from the start and are used even in this state.
the afarkes. A large funnel.
for it is like a machatz, which does not receive. It is like a large barrel without a bottom, which cannot serve as a receptacle, and therefore it is pure.
even though it receives. Since it is rounded and can serve as a receptacle.
the glass tarvad that receives. A spoon into which liquids are put.
even though when he places it on the table it tips over on its side and does not receive. Because it is round it cannot stand and tilts on its side so that the liquids spill out of it.
it is susceptible to impurity. Since it was made from the start to receive when held in the hand.

a glass serving bowl that he made into a mirror. A bowl that he made into a mirror, being glass through which one looks, and because of its rounded shape things seen through it appear distorted, smaller or larger than their true size (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 30:2).
is susceptible to impurity. It still has the law of a bowl that is susceptible to impurity, since it was made from the start as a receptacle and is not purified merely by a change of use.

and if he made it from the start as a mirror, so that things placed in it are seen from behind it, it is pure. If he made the vessel for decoration, placing attractive things inside the glass and looking at them through it, the vessel is pure even though it is a receptacle, since the purpose of the vessel from its making is to look through it and not to receive.
we have already explained in several places. Hilchot Tum'at Met 6:3, Hilchot Parah 14:1, Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 8:2, and elsewhere.

that an earthenware vessel becomes impure only from its airspace. That is, it does not become impure when impurity touches it from outside but when the impurity is in the air inside the vessel, even if it does not touch the vessel from inside. As to the reason, some explained that since clay is an inferior material, the importance of an earthenware vessel is not from its material but because it has an interior that can be used, and therefore it becomes impure only from its interior (Ralbag, end of Parashat Shemini, p. 318, and similarly see Emet VeEmunah, section 88).

or by the shifting of a zav. When a zav moves the vessel, he makes it impure even without touching it (Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 8:2). Even though an earthenware vessel does not become impure by touching its back, it becomes impure by a zav's shifting because the one who shifts is considered as touching the entire vessel, and therefore it is as if the zav touched the vessel from inside (see Hilchot Tum'at Met 6:3).
and all other utensils that impurity touched became impure. Whether the impurity touched them from outside or from inside.
what is impure in an earthenware vessel is pure in all utensils. When the impurity is in the air of the vessel.
and what is impure in all utensils is pure in an earthenware vessel. When the impurity touches the vessel from outside.

an earthenware vessel does not make utensils impure from its airspace. For the verse stated about the impurity of earthenware vessels speaks only of food and drink, as it says: "And every earthen vessel into which any of them falls, whatever is in it shall be unclean... Of all food which may be eaten... and all drink that may be drunk" (Leviticus 11:33-34).
and they again make utensils impure. For the Sages decreed that impure liquids make impure the utensils they touch (Hilchot Shear Avot HaTumot 7:2).

and this one says: your impurities did not defile me, and you defiled me. As if the vessel says to the liquid inside it: the air of the earthenware vessel that made you impure did not make me impure, but you made me impure.

an earthenware vessel that impure liquids touched on its back only, its back became impure like all other utensils. By Torah law, liquids that are not a primary source of impurity do not make utensils impure. But the Sages decreed that even liquids that became impure from a primary source and touched utensils make them impure when they touched them from inside, and they become secondary-degree impure and make terumah and sacred food impure. And if they touched them from behind, they make impure only the back of the utensils. This decree applies also to earthenware vessels, though they are usually not made impure from their backs (Hilchot Shear Avot HaTumot 7:1-3).
when it had an interior. A receptacle.
for any earthenware vessel without an interior, its back does not become impure from liquids. For it is not susceptible to impurity at all (below 18:1).

food or liquids touched the back of the impure earthenware vessel. For example, one that became impure from impurity that entered it (but if it became impure from impure liquids that touched its back, it does not make terumah food impure but only terumah liquids - see Hilchot Shear Avot HaTumot 7:6).
for earthenware vessels etc.. There is no difference between a vessel into whose airspace impurity entered and one that was turned over impurity lying on the ground.
from tradition. The Sages' received tradition for explaining verses.

a creeping creature found beneath the floor of an oven. The oven is built like a small structure on the ground and has no built bottom, but the earth beneath it is its floor, and in this earth there is a pit in which a creeping creature was found.

the oven is pure, for I say it was stillborn. For even if the creeping creature was not in the pit before the oven was built over it, and entered the oven, it may then have been alive, and a live creeping creature is not impure.

even though all utensils found are impure, as we explained. For the Sages decreed impurity on utensils that were found, lest they had become impure from a zav or a corpse (Hilchot Shear Avot HaTumot 13:4).
the oven is pure, for I say they were there before the oven came. That they were buried in the ground before the oven was built over it.

found in the ashes. In ashes taken out of the oven (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 9:3). Some explain that the utensil was found at the bottom of the oven mixed with the oven's ashes (Rash there). In these cases it is proven that the needle was inside the oven.

found in the floor of an oven, visible but not protruding into its airspace. Sunk in the ground but with their upper side exactly level with the ground, so that they can be seen but do not protrude into the cavity of the oven.
in medium dough, neither very soft nor hard. Neither so liquid that it seeps into the cracks, nor so hard that it does not stick to the wall of the oven (Commentary to the Mishnah there).

a creeping creature found in the eye of an oven. A hole in the wall of the oven near its bottom, through which fire is put in and ashes taken out, and which can be opened and closed (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 8:7); at times it protruded outward like a chimney.
kirah... kofach. For the difference between an oven, a stove and a kofach, see the explanation above 1:13.
if it was found from the inner edge outward. Under the part of the eye that protrudes outside the wall of the oven.
likewise if it was found in the airspace of the eye. Under the thickness of the oven's wall.

and even if there was an olive-bulk of a corpse there. For an olive-bulk of a corpse makes impure in a tent, and here it does not make the oven's airspace impure even though it is beneath the eye of the oven.

unless the thickness of the eye was an opening of a handbreadth. That the ceiling of the eye has a measure of a handbreadth by a handbreadth, and with such a measure the eye of the oven is considered a tent.

for it brings the impurity into the airspace of the oven. For corpse impurity passes from tent to tent through an opening (for example if the opening of the eye is a handbreadth by a handbreadth - Tiferet Yisrael, Kelim 8:8).
as explained in the matter of corpse impurity. Hilchot Tum'at Met 12:1.
the creeping creature was found in the place where the wood is put. An opening at the bottom of the stove through which the fire is taken out (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 8:8).
found in the place where the bath attendant sits. Who heats the water for the bathhouse.
in the place where the dyer sits. Who dyes cloth by boiling it in water with dye.
in the place where the olive boilers sit. Boilers of the hard olives whose oil does not come out in the olive press (Tiferet Yisrael there).
all is pure. For all these places are outside the stove.
unless the impurity was found from the closed part inward. The structure of the stove itself, and not outside it or beneath the thickness of its walls.
in whose middle is a sort of earthenware grate. Like a cover.
and its upper rim, above the grate, is like a comb. Made of projections with air between them.

for this is the interior of this vessel. Even though there is no complete wall, it is considered a receptacle, since this place is a continuation of the vessel's receptacle and that is how it is used (Aruch HaShulchan 208:9).
rims. Walls.
if the inner one projected. Was higher than the other walls.

all the foods and liquids in the space between the inner rim and the middle one... are pure. For the inner rim is considered a vessel by itself, and the foods between the inner rim and the middle one, and between the middle and the outer, are outside.
if they were level. At the same height.
lapasim. A sort of small pots or deep pans.

the one with the creeping creature is impure, and the other lapasim are pure, they and all the foods in them. If the creeping creature is in the inner vessel, the outer vessel did not become impure because the creeping creature is not considered to be in the outer vessel's interior but in its inner interior. And if the creeping creature is in the outer vessel, the food in the inner vessel did not become impure because it is not considered in the outer vessel but in its inner interior (below 14:8-9). And the inner vessel itself did not become impure because utensils do not become impure from the airspace of an earthenware vessel (above halachah 3).
each lapas of them was. Of the inner vessels (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 10:8).
punctured enough to admit liquid. Punctured so that if it is placed in liquid, the liquid enters through the hole (below 19:1).

all the foods and liquids in all the lapasim are impure, for the impurity is in the airspace of all of them. For the foods and liquids are in the outer vessel together with the creeping creature, and the inner vessels do not separate since they are punctured.
as will be explained. Below 14:9.
it is impure and all the others are pure, for the creeping creature did not enter the airspace of the upper ones. But lies in the outer vessel.

and the rim of the lower one does not project so as to make impure all the foods and liquids inside it. This halachah is difficult: why does the outer vessel not make impure the liquids inside the inner vessel, when in the previous passage (and below 14:9) it says that a vessel punctured enough to admit liquid does not protect from impurity (and see Mirkevet HaMishneh and Taharat HaKelim).

if the creeping creature was in the upper one and the rim of the lower one projected. Here again it speaks of whole vessels (Rabbi Ovadiah of Bartenura, Kelim 10:8), and the creeping creature is in the inner vessel and the rim of the outer vessel is higher than the rim of the inner vessel.

and likewise the lower one, because its rim projects, the creeping creature is in its airspace. The outer vessel is impure because its rim is higher than the rim of the inner vessel and the creeping creature is considered to be inside it.

and the other lapasim inside the lower one are pure. The middle lapasim are pure because their rim is not higher than the rim of the inner vessel and the creeping creature is not considered to be in their airspace, nor do they become impure from the airspace of the outer vessel in which they are placed, since an earthenware vessel does not become impure from the airspace of an earthenware vessel.
and if there was moist liquid between them. Liquid that wets the hand that touches it.

any that has moist liquid in it is impure etc.. Any of the middle vessels that has liquid in it became impure. For the liquid became impure from the airspace of an earthenware vessel and makes impure the vessel that touches it.
a tablet. A board, a tray.
that had bowls attached to it at the start of its making. The tablet and the bowls were formed as one utensil and not as two utensils glued together.
and if the tablet had a projecting wall so that all the bowls were inside it. A raised wall surrounding all the bowls.
and likewise the law of an earthenware spice box. A spice vessel divided into compartments so that the spices do not mix with one another.
and matching inkwells. An inkwell divided into two parts.

a wooden spice box one of whose compartments became impure through liquids. For purposes of impurity from liquids, the law of wooden utensils is similar to that of earthenware: liquids that make impure by rabbinic decree make all utensils impure only from inside them, but if the liquids fell on the back of the utensil only its back became impure (see above halachah 4).
the other compartments did not become impure. Because the liquids did not fall into them.

and if it has a projecting wall etc.. That all that is within the projecting wall is considered the interior of one utensil, and all of it becomes impure when liquids fall into it. But if a creeping creature fell into the utensil, all the compartments became impure even if it had no projecting rim, because a creeping creature makes utensils impure even from their backs, and therefore when the creeping creature is in one compartment it touches the backs of the other compartments and they all became impure.

if its compartments were. It seems this speaks of wooden utensils that became impure through a creeping creature, which become impure both from inside and from the back, and the question is whether the compartments are considered one utensil. In the previous passage it spoke of impurity from liquids, which make impure only from inside the utensil, and then it is not enough that the compartments are joined to one another, but they must have a projecting rim so that they are all considered the interior of one utensil (based on Tosefta, Kelim Bava Kamma 2:7, and see Kesef Mishneh, who explained differently).
fixed. Attached.

these are a connection to one another for impurity and for sprinkling. That if one compartment became impure, all the compartments became impure, and if they became impure through a corpse and the ashes of the red heifer were sprinkled on one of them, all became pure.
if they were only wedged. Joined by pressure without nails.

these are a connection for impurity and are not a connection for sprinkling. For such a connection does not truly make the compartments one utensil, and therefore they are not a connection for sprinkling.
and if its compartments were removable. That one takes them out and puts them back.

whatever protects with a tightly bound cover in a tent of a corpse protects with a tightly bound cover in the airspace of an earthenware vessel. A tent containing a corpse makes impure everything inside it. But if it contains an earthenware vessel or a vessel not susceptible to impurity that has a tight, firm cover on it, it protects what is inside from becoming impure from the air (Hilchot Tum'at Met 21:1).

and whatever does not protect in a tent of a corpse does not protect in the airspace of an earthenware vessel. For details of the laws of the tightly bound cover in a tent of a corpse see there, chapters 21-22.

and just as there is no tightly bound cover for impurity in a tent of a corpse. A vessel surrounded by a tightly bound cover protects what is inside it from becoming impure, but does not prevent the impurity inside it from making impure what is outside it (Hilchot Tum'at Met 20:1).
an impure ring that was embedded in a brick. For example, it was in the clay when it was fired and became a brick (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 9:6).
even though if a loaf of terumah touched this wood or this brick it is pure. For it did not touch the impure ring and needle but the brick and the wood.

they make an earthenware vessel impure from its airspace. For an earthenware vessel becomes impure when the impurity is in its airspace even without contact, and here the ring or needle is in the airspace of the earthenware vessel.
and if the rooster died there, the oven became impure. But if the creeping creature was digested in the rooster's intestines, it no longer makes impure (see Hilchot Tum'at Met 20:4).

for what is swallowed in a living creature protects from an earthenware vessel as it protects in a tent of a corpse. Impurity swallowed in a living animal or person does not make impure in a tent or in an earthenware vessel, but if the animal dies, the impurity is no longer considered swallowed (there, halachah 2).
in the folds. Between the folds of flesh.
and he closed his mouth. He shut his mouth.
he had in his fold a lentil-bulk of a creeping creature. Which is the measure for impurity (Hilchot Shear Avot HaTumot 4:2).
potsherds. Pieces of earthenware.
that impure liquids were used on and dried. The liquids were absorbed into the potsherds.
and they fell into the airspace of an earthenware vessel, they did not make it impure. For liquids absorbed in earthenware do not come out on their own, except by firing in an oven.
with minor liquids. Liquids that are first-degree impure.
but if severe liquids were absorbed in them etc.. Those that are a primary source of impurity.
and he was particular that it come out. That he wants the liquids to come out.
in fresh pomace. Moist waste left from olives that were pressed.

that came from impure liquids. For example, an impure person pressed the olives, and the oil and juice that came out of the olives became impure and were absorbed back into the pomace (Tosefta, Kelim Bava Kamma 6:18).
but in old, it is pure. For it has already dried and has no absorbed liquid.
dried. Dry.

if it fell into the airspace of an earthenware vessel it made it impure, for the liquid is destined to come out. For it is the way of liquids to come out of a sponge, so the liquid is regarded as lying in a container and not as absorbed, and makes the oven impure. If the liquid is not destined to come out, it does not make the oven impure. Even though nothing is considered absorbed except in living creatures (above halachah 4), the law of liquids differs because when they are absorbed they are completely nullified within the thing in which they were absorbed, and therefore absorption in utensils protects them from making impure (see Tosafot Anshei Shem, Kelim 9:4, Chazon Ish, Kelim Bava Kamma 6:19, Chazon Ish, Kelim 11:20).
and likewise a piece of turnip and of reed. Turnip and a cord made of reed grass that absorbed impure liquids have the law of a sponge.
an earthenware vessel that was divided in half... the whole vessel became impure. Even though the two parts are entirely separated by the partition.

because people do not divide earthenware vessels the way tents are divided. Even though in a tent of a corpse a partition is effective under certain conditions, and a corpse on one side does not make impure what is on the other side (see Hilchot Tum'at Met 24:2). In an earthenware vessel the partition is ineffective since it is not customary to divide vessels, and the entire cavity of the vessel is considered one place.
even though the impurity is enclosed within an earthenware vessel. That the impurity is in the inner part of the vessel, which is inside the outer vessel.
if it was in a vessel of wood, metal, or the like. Utensils that have purification in a mikveh, such as wooden utensils.
with a hole the size to let olives out. A hole through which an olive can come out.
whose measure is that it admits liquid. That if the vessel is placed in liquid, the liquid enters the vessel through the hole (below 19:1).

one stopped the hole of an earthenware vessel etc.. An earthenware vessel whose rim is higher than the rim of the oven and which has a hole plugged with pitch is not considered a whole vessel for purposes of its interior being treated as separate from the interior of the oven. But since an earthenware vessel protects in a tent of a corpse when it is sealed with pitch by the law of a tightly bound cover, the sealing with pitch is effective to consider the hole as plugged, and it has the law of a vessel surrounded by a tightly bound cover, which does not prevent the impurity inside it from making impure but protects what is in it from becoming impure (Chazon Ish, Kelim Bava Kamma 3:4).
as we explained. Above halachah 2.
and all other utensils. That are not earthenware vessels.

does not protect from an earthenware vessel. They do not protect what is in them from becoming impure from the airspace of an earthenware vessel, for since they do not protect with a tightly bound cover in a tent of a corpse, plugging with pitch is of no use in them at all.
a leaky gourd. That has a hole in it.

the wineskin and the kefishah. The wineskin is a leather bag, and perhaps the kefishah mentioned here too is a utensil made of leather (see Rashi, Chullin 107a; however a kefishah is found made of other materials as well - see Commentary to the Mishnah, Tevul Yom 2:4).

even though they are nullified from the status of utensils, they protect from an earthenware vessel. Since one can cut off the part in which the hole is and use the rest of the wineskin or kefishah as a new utensil, when the hole is above the rim of the outer vessel it is regarded as if it were cut off and the remainder of the wineskin or kefishah is a new utensil that protects from impurity (Chazon Ish, Kelim Bava Kamma 6:12; and perhaps this law holds for all utensils, so that if the hole is above the rim of the outer vessel the punctured vessel protects from impurity - see Sidrei Taharot, Kelim 96:1).
a flat hide. A flat hide that has no receptacle.
from the floor of an oven. The bottom of the oven.
once they are fired in a kiln. Once they are baked and hardened in a kiln. Before that they are earthen vessels and are not susceptible to impurity (above 1:6).

the oven etc.. The oven, the stove and the kofach differ from other earthenware vessels in that they are susceptible to impurity even when attached to the ground (below halachah 6), and their completion is by lighting a fire in them in order to bake in them.

once he has heated it enough to bake sufganin in it. The oven is made as a cylinder or cone and has room to put one pot on it, and one also bakes inside it by sticking the bread to its inner walls. The completion of the oven is when it is heated until it is hot enough to bake sufganin in it, which are soft, puffy baked goods. A new oven requires prolonged heating to reach such heat (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 5:1).
the stove. Made as a rectangle and has room to put two pots on it.
once he has heated it enough to cook on it a beaten hen's egg. Mixed and fried in oil.
and placed in a pan. A deep pan.
the kofach. A square vessel with room to put one pot on it, and some use it for baking.
if it was large. Whose width and thickness are like those of a large oven in which one roasts and bakes.
once he begins it with four handbreadths. Once he builds it to a height of four handbreadths, even though he intends to add to it.
an oven that was heated from behind. From outside.
or that was heated unknowingly. Unintentionally.
or that was heated from the builder's house. The oven builder heated the oven not in order to bake in it.
to roast in it. He does not stick bread and the like to its walls, but hangs meat in its cavity for roasting.
to bleach flax bundles in it. They would soak bundles of flax threads in a pot with water, and then place the pot with the flax in the oven so that it would heat up and bleach.

for this does not do work with the body of the oven. For bleaching flax there is no need for the walls of the oven to preserve the heat of the cavity as in roasting and baking, only for the fire beneath the pot (Chiddushei HaRambam, Kelim Bava Kamma 4:4). Some explain that for bleaching flax the oven's heat must be low, and heating meant to bring the oven to such a heat is not considered the heating by which the oven's work is completed (Rambam LeAm; and see Aruch HaShulchan 211:13 and Chazon Ish, Kelim 7:16, who explain in other ways).
an oven that was divided in two. He made a partition in the middle of the oven before the oven was heated and its work completed.
and one of its parts was heated and became impure through liquids. Which make utensils impure by rabbinic law.
it is impure and its companion is pure. For the Sages did not decree that the liquids make impure anything but the part whose work was completed and which is fit to become impure.

it became impure through a creeping creature and the like, impurities of the Torah, all is impure. For with impurity that is from the Torah, the whole oven is regarded as one utensil and all of it is impure (Aruch HaShulchan 212:2).
and the thickness between them. The partition between the two parts of the oven.
and one of them became impure through liquids in its airspace. That impure liquids were in the airspace of the vessel.
but if he heated it and afterward divided it... all became impure. For the entire oven is considered one utensil, and the partition made afterward is ineffective.
and they are impure as metal utensils. Their laws of impurity are the same as those of metal utensils.

and not when attached to the ground, like an oven and stoves. An earthenware oven and stoves are impure even when attached to the ground, but a metal oven is not susceptible to impurity when attached to the ground.

and if they became impure through a corpse they become a primary source of impurity like other metal utensils. But an earthenware vessel that touched a corpse does not become a primary source of impurity but only first-degree (Hilchot Tum'at Met 5:6).
and sealed it with clay. He filled the hole with clay.
a coating of clay. A layer of clay on the outside to plug the crack.
an addition of clay. An addition to the rim of the oven that was chipped (see Mishnah Acharonah, Kelim 5:11).
so that the fire comes out through it. So that the fire exits through the hole.
petpotin. Legs serving as a tripod for the pot.
becomes impure as a stove. Although the stove is mainly of metal, the earthenware petpotin make it a stove of earthenware.

he plastered it with clay, whether inside or outside, it is still not susceptible to impurity. As an earthenware vessel, but as a metal vessel. For on a stove, which is used for cooking by placing the pot on it, there is no need to retain the heat inside it, but it suffices that a fire can be lit in it, and plastering with clay is not essential to its use. But in an oven in which bread is baked, its heat must be well retained, and therefore plastering it with clay is essential to its use and makes it an earthenware vessel (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 5:11).
a metalworkers' crucible. An oven or pit coated with clay in which the smiths melt metal.
that has a place for a pot. A place to set a pot.
becomes impure as a stove. For only ovens and stoves made for cooking food are susceptible to impurity (Aruch HaShulchan 212:13).
and likewise of glassmakers. Who make glass from sand.
a lime kiln. Those who burn stones to make lime from them.
and of glaziers. Shapers of glass vessels.
and of potters. Makers of earthenware. They are pure because the kiln is not made for cooking and baking.

the purnah. A baking oven in which pastries or pots are placed on the floor of the oven (unlike ordinary ovens in which the bread is stuck to their walls). Since the purnah itself is not used, it is not considered a utensil and is not susceptible to impurity.
if it has a wall, it is susceptible to impurity. For at times pots are placed on the wall, so the purnah itself is used and not only the ground (Mishnah Acharonah, Kelim 8:9).
a coating. A coating of clay.

and if he coated it only on the outside, it becomes impure by contact and does not become impure through airspace. For it is not a complete utensil but the Sages decreed impurity on it, and decreed that it become impure only by contact so that people would recognize that this impurity is not from the Torah and would not burn terumah and sacred food that touched such an oven (Chazon Ish, Kelim Bava Kamma 4:3, and compare below 17:5).
he attached stones to the oven and did not attach them to one another, they become impure with the oven. For they are considered part of the oven.

he attached them to one another and did not attach them to the oven, they are like a tirah. A tirah is an enclosed place in front of the oven in which the bread is placed when taken out of the oven. That place is considered part of the oven, and if the oven becomes impure the tirah becomes impure (if it is four handbreadths high, below 17:4).
he dug in the ground and made a tirah, it is pure. For it is not a utensil, and the ground does not become impure.
and a stove's tirah is pure. For one need not make a tirah for a stove, only for an oven (Gra's commentary on the Tosefta, Kelim Bava Kamma 4:2).
two barrels and two lapasim that he made into a stove. For he lights a fire between them and places the pot on the barrels or the pans.
between them it becomes impure by airspace and by contact. Like the law of a stove.
and the interior of the barrels is pure. For the interior of the barrels is like the back of the stove, and an earthenware vessel does not become impure from its back.
to set the pot on them. To put a pot on them.
even though he made a place at their top with clay. He stuck a piece of clay on the top of the nails to widen them (Rash, Kelim 6:1) or made a ring of clay joining the nails (Tiferet Yisrael there).
it is pure like a metal stove. Which is not susceptible to impurity when attached to the ground (above halachah 6). For the metal nails are the essence of the utensil.
are not susceptible to impurity, as if it were a stone stove. Above halachah 6.
one who makes two stones a stove etc.. For with stones that are large, two suffice, but with petpotin, which are small, three are needed (Tiferet Yisrael, Kelim 6:1).
and joined them with clay. He attached them to the ground with clay (and likewise plastered them with clay, as explained in the previous halachah).
is not susceptible to impurity. Even the stone attached with clay does not become impure, for this is not a stove.
the stone. Attached to the ground with clay (Rash, Kelim 6:2).

on it and on the oven etc.. The stone is slightly apart from the oven and he places the pot partly on the stone and partly on the oven, and likewise with a stove and a kofach. In all these the stone is considered part of the oven, kofach or stove, which are susceptible to impurity in their own right.
the rock. A stone naturally attached to the ground (Rash, Kelim 6:2).

is not susceptible to impurity. For the rock or the wall is not a utensil and is not susceptible to impurity, and the stone attached with clay does not become impure because fewer than two stones attached with clay are not a stove, as explained above halachah 14.
the butchers' stove etc.. Sellers of cooked meat who arrange a row of stones to place many pots on them, each pot resting on two stones.
one of them became impure. That impurity entered the airspace between two stones.
not all of them became impure. For every two stones are considered a stove by themselves.

three stones that he joined with clay and made two stoves. He set them up and joined them side by side and the pot rests on two stones, and the middle stone is wide and serves with each of the outer stones as a separate cooking place.

if the outer stone of the pure stove was removed, the entire middle one is definitely impure. The whole middle stone becomes impure because the pure stove was nullified and it serves only the impure stove.

if one can set a large cauldron on the two outer ones, they are impure etc.. If a large pot can be placed on the two outer stones, they are still like one large stove and impure. If they are farther apart, they cannot be used as a stove and are pure.
he returned the middle one, all is pure as it was. For returning the stone without plastering it with clay is not considered building the stove anew.
provided he heats it for each of them enough to cook an egg on it. Like the law of a new stove, which requires heating (above halachah 1).
half of each stone of the first stove is impure etc.. The inner half of each stone of the stove is impure, since it is part of the inner impure stove.
and half of the stone is pure. The outer half is pure, since it is part of the outer pure stove.
an earthenware duchan. A rectangular, hollow earthenware vessel whose upper part is perforated. It is filled with hot embers and the pots are placed on it after cooking.
pure as a stove and impure as a receptacle. It is considered a receptacle and not a stove, since it is not used for cooking but to keep the pots warm.

and if it was punctured it is not susceptible to impurity as a receptacle, unlike a stove. For a punctured or broken stove remains susceptible to impurity until it falls below a height of three fingerbreadths (below 16:1).

its sides, one who touches them is not impure as a stove. The Rambam's words are not entirely clear, and perhaps it speaks of a duchan standing next to a stove; though parts adjacent to a stove sometimes become impure with it (such as the stove's courtyard - below 17:6), the sides of the duchan facing the stove are not considered part of the stove and do not become impure with it.
its wide part on which one sits while the dish cooks. A flat place attached to the duchan and used for sitting.
becomes impure if the duchan became impure. It is considered part of the duchan and not part of the stove.
likewise one who inverts a basket and builds a stove on it. He turned over a wooden basket and built a stove on it.
it is impure as a wooden utensil, not as a stove. The basket is impure by the law of a wooden utensil and not by the law of the stove, even though the stove is built on it.
a large oven... and the small one. See above 15:2.
if four handbreadths remain in the large one. Of the height of the oven.
and in the small, most of it. That most of the oven's height remains.
to break it. To shatter it, since an earthenware vessel is not purified by immersion but only by breaking.
divided into three parts. He cuts the oven from top to bottom so that the circumference of the oven is divided into three.
and scrapes off the coating. Removes the clay coating.
for it is impossible to determine. It is impossible to measure precisely which of the parts is larger.
an earthenware tablet with a rim that was divided in two. An earthenware tray with a frame that broke, and its parts can still be used for serving although its frame is not whole.
pure. If it was divided into equal parts (for the reason, see Tiferet Yisrael, Kelim 12:6, Sidrei Taharot, Kelim 130:1, Aruch HaShulchan 214:7-12).
and one large like two, the large one is impure. Since it is then most of the oven.
provided he heats it. Like the completion of work of a new oven (above 15:1).
he distanced the coating from it etc.. He assembled the sections, put sand or small stones on them, and over the sand coated it with a clay coating.
is never susceptible to impurity. Because on the oven itself there is no clay joining the sections to one another.

if it had one section with four handbreadths, it becomes impure by contact and does not become impure through airspace. For this impurity is rabbinic, and to make a mark that this impurity is rabbinic they decreed that it become impure by contact and not by airspace (Chazon Ish, Kelim Bava Kamma 14:4, and compare below 17:5).
an oven that came in pieces from the craftsman's house. The potter made it in many pieces like columns meant to be fitted to one another.
and made supports that gather it to be as one. He made on the outside a kind of hoops or props that press the standing pieces together, thus forming the circumference of the oven.
when he removes the supports it becomes pure. For removing the hoops is like breaking the oven.
and even if he replaced them it is pure. For after the oven has been heated, one cannot join the parts tightly (Chiddushei HaRitva, Bava Metzia 59a).

and he need not heat it, for it was already heated. It is not like an oven that was entirely broken and repaired, which requires heating anew, but it suffices that it was heated before the plastering.
an oven that he cut into sections. Widthwise.

and put sand between section and section and plastered all of it with clay on the outside. He puts down a section and sand on it and sets the next section on the sand until he completes the shape of the oven, and then plasters all of it with clay on the outside and joins all of it.
it is susceptible to impurity. Even though sand separates one section from the next, since the clay adheres to all the sections on the outside it joins them into a complete oven.
an Arabs' pit, which he digs in the ground and plasters with clay. The walls of the pit, and the pit is heated and afterward bread is baked in it.
if the clay can stand by itself. Without the earth around it.
and if not, it is pure. For it is nullified and considered part of the ground.
a pates. A large earthenware vessel, like a barrel.
whose bottom he broke. That he broke its bottom so that it would serve as an oven.

even though it receives on its walls the measure. A broken earthenware vessel is still susceptible to impurity if, when tilted on its side, it holds liquids to a certain measure (explained below 18:14). But the pates, since he made it an oven, is nullified from being a utensil and is not susceptible to impurity even when it holds liquids, and it is not susceptible as an oven either, since it still needs to be coated on the inside (Chazon Ish, Kelim Bava Kamma 4:16).
an oven of cracks etc.. An oven made of pieces of earthenware joined to one another, each piece coated with clay, but the places of the cracks were not coated.
is not susceptible to impurity. For the parts are not connected to one another and are considered fragments of vessels (Chazon Ish, Kelim Bava Kamma 4:10).
gypsum. Plaster.
clay. Crushed potsherds mixed with water and made into dough.
a crack of an oven. A gap between the parts of the oven.
that he set toward a corner. He placed the oven facing the corner of the house, and the oven touches two walls so that the crack is in the space between the walls and the oven.
and plastered with clay from the sides. At the joint between the walls and the oven, so that the heat of the oven is retained, but he did not plaster over the crack itself.
pure. For the oven itself is not joined and is considered demolished (Aruch HaShulchan 215:13).
a board of an oven. A piece of the oven's wall.
that he set in the corners to bake in it is pure. For it is like fragments of an oven, and the walls do not help to make it a complete oven.
and if it has most of an oven, it is susceptible to impurity. As explained above halachah 3.

becomes impure only from the earth upward. And the lower half of the oven is pure, since once he filled it with earth it was nullified from being an oven and has the law of an ordinary earthenware vessel attached to the ground, which is pure.

and if it became impure by contact and impurity touched it from inside, all of it became impure, even from the earth downward. For although the lower part is pure, the Sages decreed impurity on it, and to distinguish between impurity from the Sages and impurity from the Torah they decreed that it become impure only by contact and not by airspace (Or Sameach, Aruch HaShulchan 215:14 and as below 17:5; but see Sidrei Taharot, Kelim 87:1, who explains differently).
a stove divided lengthwise is pure. For one cannot place pots on it at all.
and widthwise it is still susceptible to impurity. For one pot can be placed on it.
the kalatot. A kind of round base on which the stove is placed. The wood and coals lie on the kalat and from there their heat rises to the stove above them.
whose bottom sank. A depression formed in the kalat.
and it does not cook. It does not cook well the food on top of the stove.
he put a stone or pebble on the depression. To raise the fire.
its handle, which it needs in its use. The handles of utensils, or any other part that is not part of the utensil's body but assists in the work done with the utensil.
as will be explained. Below chapter 20.
therefore the stone. That serves to thicken the wall of the oven and is attached to it with clay (Rash, Kelim 5:2).
that protrudes a handbreadth from the oven. Projects outward from the oven's wall, and the measure of the projection is a handbreadth.
a connection. For the stone thickens the oven and helps preserve its heat (Commentary to the Mishnah there).

and if they touched beyond a handbreadth of an oven or beyond three fingerbreadths of a stove, they are pure. For beyond a handbreadth or three fingerbreadths the stone is no longer needed to preserve the heat.
the oven's addition. A layer of clay added above the upper rim of the oven to raise it.
that of householders is pure. Since they do not use the added part.
and that of bakers is impure with the oven's impurity, because he leans the spit on it. Of meat, so that it does not cool until the buyers come (Tiferet Yisrael, Kelim 5:5).
the addition of a cauldron. An addition of clay to the rim of the cauldron, which is a pot built into the ground and usually made of copper (Commentary to the Mishnah there).
that of olive boilers is impure. For the cauldron's addition stops the boiling olives from spilling over when they boil.

and that of dyers is pure. For the cauldron's addition, being made of clay, spoils the dye, and therefore dyers do not fill the cauldron to its rim, so that the dye will not spill over and be spoiled, and so they do not use the cauldron's addition (Rash and Tiferet Yisrael there).
a stove's crown. A kind of frame on top of the stove for setting the pots in it and keeping them warm.

pure. Some explain that because a crown is not usually made for a stove, the crown is not part of the stove and not a connection to it (Rash, Kelim 5:3). Others explain that because its benefit in preserving heat is slight, it is not considered a handle of the stove (Tiferet Yisrael there).

when it is four handbreadths high it is impure with the oven's impurity. The commentators wondered (Mishnah Acharonah, Kelim 5:3, Chazon Ish, Kelim 7:11) why the tirah is impure if it is not attached to the oven. It may be explained that the air between them is considered the interior of one utensil, similar to three petpotin or stove stones, which are considered one utensil even though they are not attached to one another (above 15:13).

less than this is pure because it is not a connection to it. Because at such a height the tirah is not fit for placing bread in it and does not serve the oven's needs, and therefore it is not considered attached to it.

and if he attached it to the oven, even on three stones, it is impure. For the act of attaching proves that the person wants the tirah to be part of the oven. Therefore even if he attached it to the oven by setting it on three stones, so that it does not stand stably, it is impure.
a flask-place. A place next to the stove in which a flask of oil is placed.
and a spice place. A place for placing spice.
and a lamp place. A place for placing a lamp.
if the stove became impure by contact. That a creeping creature touched it.
and if it became impure through airspace. That a creeping creature entered the airspace of the stove.

they did not become impure, because they are a connection to it only by rabbinic decree. For these places are not one utensil with the stove, since they are not needed by it and do not serve it, but because they are attached to it the Sages decreed that they be considered attached.

so that terumah and sacred food not be burned on account of their touching. It is forbidden to destroy terumah or sacred food, but terumah and sacred food that became impure by Torah law must be burned. With things impure only by rabbinic decree, which it is forbidden to destroy, they feared people would come to burn them, so they instituted a mark and distinction in this impurity so that people would know it is only rabbinic and would not burn terumah and sacred food on account of this impurity.
but are left in suspense. Neither eaten nor burned.
the stove's courtyard. A walled earthenware surface built in front of the stove's opening and attached to it.

if the courtyard was less than this etc.. Below three fingerbreadths the stove's courtyard is not considered a utensil, like the stove itself, which is not susceptible to impurity below three fingerbreadths (above 15:2, 16:1), but the Sages decreed impurity on it because it is attached to the stove (Rash, Kelim 7:3).

but if one of them became impure only from its airspace, its companion is not impure. If the impurity was only in the airspace of the courtyard, the stove did not become impure, and if the impurity was in the airspace of the stove at a place higher than the height of the courtyard's walls, only the stove became impure. But if the impurity was in the airspace of the stove below the height of the courtyard's rim, both the courtyard and the stove became impure, because this place is considered the airspace of both (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 7:3, Mirkevet HaMishneh).
if the stove's courtyard was set apart from the stove. Not attached to the stove.
when it is three fingerbreadths high, it is a connection to it. As with the oven's tirah above, halachah 4.
or if the courtyard was smooth and had no rim. That the courtyard is only a surface of earthenware with no walls at all, on which pots and the like can be placed, and it serves the stove.

the stove's petpotin are three. Projections extending from the stove on which the pot is placed are considered part of the stove and become impure with it. Fewer than three petpotin are not considered part of the stove, as explained further in the halachah.
the height of each of them was three fingerbreadths or less. So they are like the body of the stove.
and likewise if there were four. Even if there were four petpotin, all are impure, although three petpotin suffice to support the stove.

he made for it two petpotin opposite each other. A pot does not sit well on two petpotin and they are fit for use only with difficulty, and therefore they are not impure by Torah law but by rabbinic decree.

and from three upward etc.. At a length of more than three fingerbreadths they are not part of the stove (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 7:4), and are impure by rabbinic decree only because they are attached to it (like the stove's courtyard above halachah 6).
if the petpotin were pulled out from the rim. Projecting beyond the rim of the stove.

and we are not exacting in all these measures, for all are rabbinic. The measure of three fingerbreadths can be measured with the fingers pressed tightly together ('atzavot') or slightly apart ('sochakot'). When it concerns Torah law one measures stringently, whereas the measures mentioned here, which concern rabbinic matters, are measured leniently (see Hilchot Shabbat 17:36, Hilchot Kilayim 8:12).
or that it receives but was not made to receive. That the utensil has a receptacle but the utensil's use and purpose is not to receive things in it.
is not susceptible to impurity at all. See above 1:8.
and the lamp. On which clay or metal lamps are placed, but which itself has no receptacle (see above 1:8).
the channels. Pipes, gutters.
even though they are bent and even though they receive. That the pipes are twisted so that water can stand in them and not only pass through.
a barrel of acacia wood. A barrel whose mouth is sealed and which serves as a float.

and a barrel sunk in the base of the machatz. The machatz is a large earthenware vessel, and at its bottom a small barrel is sunk with its mouth facing outward, so as to insert the hand from outside and lift the machatz with it, and this use does not make it a receptacle.
a lantern. A perforated vessel into which a lamp is put so that the wind does not extinguish it, and it has holes from which the light comes out.
and likewise the potters' stand that has an interior is impure. The stones on which the craftsman makes vessels from clay; sometimes they have a frame, and then they are susceptible to impurity.
because he tilts it on its side. So that the perfume does not spill.
and gives the buyer to smell with it. He lets the buyer smell the oil or perfume he sells, and so the peddler's funnel serves as a receptacle.
that were not made to receive. That were not made for use inside them but for covering.
the lapas. A kind of small pot or deep pan.

when it is perforated and has a point, it is pure. If the cover is perforated or has a handle on its back that prevents setting the lapas down upside down without tilting it on its side, it is pure, since food cannot be placed in it but it is used only as a cover.
this is the rule: anything used as an earthenware vessel while inverted is pure. For it is used upside down, and is not used to receive.

titeros. A vessel for sprinkling water, with a perforated bottom and a narrow upper opening. When one stops the opening with a finger and prevents air from entering the vessel, the water stays in the vessel, and when one removes the finger the water comes out through the holes.
even though it is perforated and lets out perutot. The water comes out of it drop by drop, like perutot coming out of a crack in a collection box (Kesef Mishneh).

the earthenware torch. A stick with a small bowl at its head in which rags soaked in oil are placed and burned. Even though it cannot stand by itself, it is susceptible to impurity because it receives and that is how it is used (see Rash, Kelim 2:8).
gastra. A broken earthenware vessel that serves as a base catching liquids for large vessels.
even though it receives. That it has a receptacle.

for a ship is not included among the utensils mentioned in the Torah. This law is based on the verse "the way of a ship in the midst of the sea" (Proverbs 30:19): just as the sea is pure, so is the ship pure (Mishnah Shabbat 9:2).

all utensils that broke and whose form was ruined, their fragments are not susceptible to impurity, even though those fragments are fit for use etc.. Although in wooden and metal utensils too, if the utensil broke and does work similar to its work, it is susceptible to impurity (above 6:1, 11:2-3), it is a novelty regarding earthenware that even though the form of the vessel was ruined and the fragment has no form of a vessel at all and cannot serve as an actual vessel but only as a gastra beneath vessels, it is nevertheless susceptible to impurity (Mirkevet HaMishneh, Aruch HaShulchan 217:7, as an answer to the difficulty raised by the Raavad).
from tradition. The Sages' tradition in explaining the verses.
only to include fragments of earthenware vessels. For when they receive, they are considered a small vessel (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 2:2).
when this potsherd had an interior to hold liquids when the potsherd sits unsupported. That it can hold liquids when it lies without support.
the potsherd that cannot sit so as to receive. That cannot sit and hold liquids without support.
because of its handle. A handle for gripping.
a point. A projection.
even though the handle was removed or the point broken. And now the potsherd can sit and hold liquids.

whose bases are pointed like the basins. That the bottom of the vessel is pointed, like the basins used for throwing blood in the Temple, which were made so that they could not be set down, so the blood would not congeal.
that broke and their bases receive. For example, that the vessel was divided in two and the bottom part remained whole.
the kripiyot. Vessels coming from Corfu.
and the bases of cups. Cups they used to make in Sidon, whose bases were pointed (Mishnah Kelim 4:3).

these are susceptible to impurity, for they were made so from the start that they receive with support or with gripping. Therefore when a fragment of them remains it is susceptible to impurity even if it cannot hold liquids without support.

enough to anoint a small person, up to barrels that hold a se'ah. If the fragment was from a vessel that held an amount between the measure of oil sufficient to anoint the body of a child and the measure of a se'ah (about 7 liters).
between their bottoms. The base of the vessel.
a revi'it. A quarter of a log (about 75 ml).
holding two se'ah or more. Somewhat more than this.
large jugs. The largest jars (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 2:2).

if the potsherds hold less than these measures, they are not susceptible to impurity. For with small vessels people take care of the fragments even when small and use them, but a large vessel that broke, its fragments are not used unless they are large.
and it was very pointed. That the bottom of the vessel is shaped like a triangle sitting on its apex, from which straight walls go up.
so that it is like a small vessel. Even though the walls broke, the bottom of the vessel does not look like a fragment but like a small vessel.
it is susceptible to impurity. Even though it does not hold a revi'it, for the law of a revi'it applies only to what looks like a fragment of a vessel.
because the walls of these vessels and the like are straight. The walls are straight and have no receptacle, whereas the vessels discussed until now have rounded walls and a receptacle.

the presumption regarding potsherds that are found etc.. Fragments of vessels that were found and it is unknown what the size of the original vessel was, for example the fragment is the size of a revi'it and it is unknown whether it broke from a vessel of a se'ah, which is susceptible to impurity, or from a vessel of two se'ah, which is not. The fragment is pure, for presumably it was discarded because it broke from a large vessel and so they gave it no importance. But the potter, in whose work many fragments arise, makes use of the surplus and uses most of the fragments, placing them under vessels to catch the liquids dripping from the vessel (above halachah 8, and see Mirkevet HaMishneh, Sidrei Taharot, Kelim 80:1, and the Gra's commentary on the Tosefta, Kelim Bava Kamma 3:4, who explained this halachah in different ways).
one made for foods, once it is punctured with an olive-passing hole. For then it is no longer fit for its work.
one made for both. Used for food and drink (compare above 14:9).
and they did not say with a liquid-emitting hole. A hole through which liquids can come out, whose measure is smaller than a hole that admits liquids.

only for a gastra, because it is made to receive liquids dripping from vessels. The measure of the vessel for purity is by what admits liquid and not by what emits liquid, because even if liquid leaks out of a vessel, one puts a gastra beneath it to catch the leaking liquid and continues to use it. But a gastra from which the liquid leaks is no longer fit to serve as a base for a vessel, and so it is pure when punctured with a liquid-emitting hole (and see below halachah 9).

and it is still considered a utensil for sanctifying purification water. For purifying one impure from a corpse, one takes living water in a vessel and puts in it the ashes of the red heifer, and sprinkles on the impure person (Hilchot Parah 6:1). If the vessel was punctured with a liquid-emitting hole it is still a vessel and valid for sanctifying purification water, but with a liquid-admitting hole it is not considered a vessel for this purpose (there 6:6).

and it is still considered a utensil for making seeds fit to receive impurity through liquids detached in it, as we explained. All seeds and foods are not susceptible to impurity until water detached from the ground comes upon them. If the water is in a vessel resting on the ground, even if it has a liquid-admitting hole, the water is considered detached and makes fit to receive impurity (Hilchot Tum'at Ochalin 2:8-9).
a hole the size of a small root. The thickness of a thin root.
the water in it does not make the seeds fit. For such a vessel is considered attached to the ground and the water in it is not considered detached (there).
and it is still a vessel for holding olives in it and is susceptible to impurity. If the vessel is made for foods, as above halachah 1.

and it is still considered a vessel for protecting with a tightly bound cover until most of it is missing, as we explained regarding corpse impurity. An earthenware vessel or a vessel not susceptible to impurity placed in a tent of a corpse, with a tight, firm cover on it, protects what is in it from becoming impure (see Hilchot Tum'at Met 20:1, 21:1). If most of the earthenware vessel is missing, it no longer protects what is in it even when he plugged the hole (there 23:3). This speaks of a large vessel, but for a small vessel the measure is the size of a pomegranate-passing hole (there).

the barrel, whose measure is with nuts. And not with olives, because people are accustomed to put larger things in it than in an ordinary vessel, and it is fit for its work even when punctured with an olive-passing hole (see Mishnah Acharonah, Kelim 3:2).
a trough. A large vessel, like a tub.
which was not made for this from the start. But was made for kneading in it while sitting in its usual way, and when it cannot be used this way its use is nullified and it is pure.

the flask and the tani. Oil vessels, except that the tani is a vessel with a narrow mouth from which the oil drips (and in Mishnah Kelim 3:2 the reading is 'hatfi', from the dripping - Commentary to the Mishnah there).
whose measure is with oil. When they are punctured with a liquid-admitting or liquid-emitting hole one estimates whether oil can come out or enter them.
and the tzartzur. Above 13:10.
whose measure is with water. Water needs a smaller hole than oil to enter or exit the vessel.
a lamp whose mouth was removed. The opening through which the wick comes out was broken.
and of earth, whose mouth was fired with the wick. And its mouth became hard like earthenware.
a barrel that was cracked. Punctured in its bottom so that it cannot hold food or drink when standing in its usual way, but when tilted on its side the depression in the barrel's wall can hold.
or that was split. Broken along its entire length and made into something like two troughs.
became loose. Weakened and cracked.
and cannot be carried with half a kav of dried figs. For if one carries the barrel with half a kav of dried figs in it, it will break.
a barrel whose handles were removed. The handles of the barrel.

it is like a gastra. And it is purified by a liquid-emitting hole (above halachah 2), because it is hard to carry, its first use as a vessel is nullified, and it has the law of a gastra (Rash, Kelim 4:3).
cracked below its handles, even though its handles are intact, it is a gastra. For if one tries to carry the barrel the handles would break.
and if it was made without handles from the start, it is judged as a barrel. Because from the beginning he wanted to use it as a vessel even without handles.
if it cracked after its work was completed, each gastra of it is susceptible to impurity. Like the law of fragments of earthenware vessels, which are susceptible to impurity (above 18:10).
and if it cracked before its work was completed... it is pure. For it was never a vessel, and earthenware that was never a vessel is not susceptible to impurity.

if its fragments were even and its interior reddened before its work was completed, it cracked. If the fragments are smooth and straight without projections, this is proof that the barrel split before it hardened into earthenware, for hard earthenware does not break in a straight line. Likewise if the inner part of the barrel is red, this is proof that the fire acted there directly, and from this it follows that it broke before its work was completed.
as we explained. Above halachah 1.

and if it was leaking, one does not make a gastra for a gastra. For when a vessel cracks, one places a gastra beneath it to catch the liquids leaking from it. But when the gastra cracks, one does not place a gastra under the gastra to catch the liquids, but throws away the cracked gastra and places another gastra in its place.
only the remnants of earthenware vessels. That broke from a whole vessel.
a gastra from which points projected. Hollow projections extending from the sides of the gastra.
whether it was sitting. On its bottom.
or tilted on its side. That it cannot sit on its bottom but only when tilted on its side.
whatever receives olives from the points. When the gastra sits on its bottom or on its side.

and whatever does not receive olives along with it becomes impure by contact and the part opposite it does not become impure through airspace. For it is not truly part of the gastra and becomes impure with it only by rabbinic decree (Aruch HaShulchan 220:8).

that is when the impurity touches them from inside. And not from behind, for an earthenware vessel is not susceptible to impurity from its back (except for impurity of liquids, above 13:4), but in other utensils that become impure by contact, there is no distinction whether the impurity touched their backs or their insides.
and coated it with dung. He coated the barrel on the outside with dung to strengthen it and join its parts.
if there was in them. In the broken potsherds that he glued.
a potsherd holding a revi'it. That is susceptible to impurity, for example that the vessel from which it broke was of a size between the anointing of a child and a se'ah (above 18:13).
only opposite that potsherd does it become impure through airspace. If the impurity entered the airspace of that potsherd that holds a revi'it, it became impure by the law of an earthenware vessel.
and the status of vessel was not nullified from the barrel. Even when it was punctured it was still a vessel, and therefore its fragments are susceptible to impurity like fragments of vessels.
a kumkum. A vessel for boiling and pouring hot water.
and he made it. He plugged the hole.
that cannot receive hot as cold. Because the pitch melts in the hot water.
a funnel. Meant for household use (above 18:3).
that he plugged. He plugged the bottom hole through which liquids exit.

pitch does not make it a receptacle, but a wooden funnel that he plugged is like a receptacle and is susceptible to impurity. For the funnel was never a receptacle, and to make it a receptacle plugging like the plugging of a punctured vessel does not suffice (as above halachah 14), but a significant plugging is required, and a significant plugging is with a material of the same kind as the vessel. Therefore in an earthenware funnel plugging with pitch is of no use because it is not of its kind, but in a wooden funnel it is effective because pitch is of the kind of wood (Tosefta, Kelim Bava Kamma 3:4 and the Gra's commentary there). Some explain that pitch adheres well to wood but not to earthenware, and therefore is ineffective in an earthenware funnel (Rosh, Kelim 3:4). And in a barrel that was punctured, plugging with pitch is effective (above halachah 14) because the hole in a barrel is rough and the pitch adheres to it, whereas in a funnel the hole is made on purpose and is smooth and the pitch does not adhere to it (Rash there).
we have already explained. Above 17:1.
one who coats a sound earthenware vessel. Who smears a whole, stable earthenware vessel on the outside with a sticky material.
but one who coats a shaky earthenware vessel, the coating is considered like the body of the vessel. For the shaky vessel needs the coating to remain whole.
the earthenware kruyah with which water is drawn. A vessel with which water is drawn from a well.
one who coats an earthenware vessel to cook in it, it is not a connection. For the coating is not needed.

he coated vessels to boil pitch in them, it is a connection. If he coated vessels to melt pitch in them, the coating is considered part of the vessel, because boiling pitch is done at very high heat and the coating is needed so that the vessel does not crack from the heat (Rash, Kelim 3:5).
and did. He coated all of it (Mirkevet HaMishneh, Aruch HaShulchan 221:10).
with tin. Tin.
and with plasters. Gypsum.
moist, drawn things. For example, soft, moist herbs.
the pates vessels. Large earthenware vessels.
the coating of an oven. They would coat the oven on the outside with clay or other materials to better preserve its heat and integrity.
and plugged it with more pitch than needed. He put on the hole more pitch than needed to plug it, so that if he removes part of the pitch the hole remains plugged.
a heater. A vessel for heating water.
that he coated with clay. Mud.
or with potsherd clay. Crushed potsherds mixed with water and made into dough.
for the potsherd clay does not join to the vessel. It does not adhere well.
the barrel's stopper. The barrel's cover.
that he coated with clay on it and on the barrel. To join them well, and when one wants to open the barrel one breaks the dried clay.

and if impure liquids touched the barrel. Since the barrel is sealed, impurity could not have entered it, so this speaks of impure liquids that make earthenware impure even from its back (above 13:4).
copper utensils that he pitched. He coated them on the inside with pitch.
and if for wine it is like the body of the vessel. Because wine is not preserved well in a metal vessel, and the pitch is needed to preserve the wine (Mishnah Acharonah, Kelim 3:7).

dough in the cracks of a trough that a creeping creature touched. A trough used for kneading in whose cracks dough remained, and a creeping creature touched the dough without touching the trough itself (and this speaks of a wooden trough, for an earthenware vessel becomes impure from its airspace even without contact).

since its prohibition is significant, it separates. Chametz on Passover is a severe prohibition, and so the dough stands by itself and does not become part of the trough, and touching it is not considered touching the trough.
during the rest of the year, if he was particular about it, the trough is pure. For he does not want the dough to remain and wants to remove it from the trough.
and if he wants it to remain. The dough, in order to plug the cracks, or for another reason.
the cords and straps on book wrappers. Thin ropes and straps with which the wrappers are tied around scrolls of the Torah, Prophets and Writings.
and on children's wrappers. Bibs that protect the child's clothes from getting dirty.
and likewise on a hoe, a sack and a basket. Perhaps these are straps used for carrying on the shoulder and the like.
and on a basket. A woven basket.
on the handles of earthenware vessels, even sewn. That he sews the strap around the handle of the vessel.

for they are not a connection to an earthenware vessel. They have no connection with garments by sewing, and only a complete connection by clay and the like is considered a connection for them (Chazon Ish, Kelim Bava Kamma 1:8, and similarly Aruch HaShulchan 221:19).
the back handle of an axe. The part of the axe handle that projects above the hole in the metal head.
and the excess beyond three, one who touches it is pure. For it is not needed for the axe's work.
the front handle of an axe. The part of the axe's shaft between the hand gripping the shaft and the metal head.

remnants etc.. In addition to the measures of handles that become impure with the utensil, this halachah also mentions the measures of the remnants of utensils, that is, the minimum length at which a broken utensil is still susceptible to impurity (the measures of remnants were counted in Mishnah Kelim 29:6-8 together with the measures of handles in order from shortest to longest, and so they are brought here as well).

the remnants of a compass, a handbreadth. A pargol is a compass, and it is susceptible to impurity if it broke and was shortened down to a handbreadth. Less than this is unfit for work and is not susceptible to impurity.

and the handle of a gem-cutters' mallet, a handbreadth. The handle of a tool with which precious stones are pierced and carved; when it becomes impure, only the handbreadth next to the head of the mallet is considered a connection and one who touches it is impure. But the rest of the handle is not needed for the work and one who touches it is pure.
the handle of goldsmiths' hammers, two handbreadths. The handle of the hammer of goldsmiths is two handbreadths long.
and of carpenters. Carpenters.

the remnants of the ox-goad. A wooden tool also called a mardea, at one end of which is an iron spearhead called a 'chorchur' and at the other end a nail called a 'darban' with which the animal is struck (above 11:23).

four handbreadths near the darban. If the goad broke and a length of four handbreadths remains from the side of the darban, it is still susceptible to impurity (and see in the next passage the measure of the remnants near the chorchur).
an axe with which one digs basins for water. Circles around trees so that water collects in them during irrigation.
a weeding axe. With which one weeds bark and weeds that grow around the trunks of trees.
a ben-patish. A small hammer. The hammer is a tool for breaking stones.
a splitting axe. Meant for splitting wood.
and a hoeing one. With which the earth is hoed.
a stonecutters' mallet. A tool for leveling and smoothing stones.
the remnants of the ox-goad near the metal chorchur. See the explanation at the end of the previous passage.
a householders' rake. A spoon with which a dish is stirred (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 29:8), or with which clay is scooped, or oven and stoves (Rash there).
and of lime makers. Makers of lime, who scoop it with a rake.

and any excess beyond this, if he wanted it to remain, is impure. All the measures of utensil handles mentioned are in the ordinary case, but if the owner of the utensil wanted the handle to be longer, it is considered part of the utensil and all of it becomes impure with it.
and the handle of all fire implements. Utensils whose use is by inserting them into fire.
and the spits. An iron grill for roasting meat.
even if they are long, any amount is impure. Because a person needs the entire length of the utensil to keep away from the fire.
a stick that he made a handle for an axe. Temporarily (Rash and other commentators on Kelim 20:3).
the diostar. A device on which the spinning thread is wound, made of a rod serving as an axle to which two rods are attached crosswise at right angles, around which the thread is wound.
to stretch the thread over them. To stretch the thread around them.
they are a connection during work. But not outside of work, because it is customary to remove the nail and take them apart.
he fixed the diostar in a beam. And the diostar became permanently attached.
it is susceptible to impurity. Even outside of work.
and the beam is not a connection to it. For the beam is not a utensil and not a handle of the diostar.
he made part of the beam into a diostar. He carved the end of the beam so that it would be part of the utensil.
the yoke. The pole attached to a wagon and laid lengthwise between the two animals that pull the wagon.
and the katrev. The wood laid on the necks of the animals (see the illustration above 10:5).
and the padding. Padding of leather or rags around the animal's neck so that it will not be wounded by the katrev.
and the ropes. The ropes tied to the wagon with which it is pulled.
and one who touches the chorev. A pole of wood or metal that the plowman holds while plowing.
and the knee. A tree trunk bent like a knee, to which the plow beam is attached.
and the handle. A handle attached to the plow and used to tilt it in the direction the plowman wants.
and the metal eye. An iron ring that is part of the plow's parts.

and the cheeks. Two wooden pieces at the end of the yoke (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 21:2); they may be a kind of wings attached to the plowshare, whose function is to widen the furrow after it is split and to move stones away.

and the ayraim. Parts hanging on the plow (Commentary to the Mishnah there). Some explain that they are two wooden boards mounted on the plow's frame, whose function is to crumble and remove clods of earth or stones from the furrow (Rash there).
impure. For all these parts are always joined and are considered one utensil.
and likewise a saw. A saw that has handles on both sides.
one who touches its handle on one side or the other. The two handles on the two sides of the saw.
and one who touches the string and the cord. A thread or thin rope tied at the top between the two handles of the saw.
and the arm. A piece of wood joining the two handles, parallel to the metal teeth of the saw.
and the connectors. Small wooden projections with which the saw's teeth are attached to the handles.
but one who touches the frame of the large saw. A rectangular wooden frame that a large saw has.
a press. A device for straightening wood. The crooked wood is placed between two boards pressed together by a screw or metal clamps.
of which the spearhead became impure. The metal part.
one who touches the press is pure. Apparently because they were accustomed to separate the spearhead from the boards, and they are not considered one utensil.

one who touches the kashtanit that is wound around it. A bow-shaped device with which a drill is turned. The bowstring is wound around the drill, and by moving the bow back and forth the drill rotates.
one who touches the string and the bow. The string or the bow itself.
pure, even when it is drawn. When the arrow is drawn in the bow, they are like two different utensils and not one utensil.
and likewise the mole trap. A mole trap made of a bow in which an arrow is drawn, and when the mole enters the trap the arrow is shot and kills it.
and likewise a stretched warp. Warp and weft threads stretched on the loom in the middle of the weaving process.
that became impure during the weaving. The part already woven to the measure of three fingerbreadths and fit to receive impurity became impure (below 22:12).
one who touches the upper beam and the lower beam. The loom is made of two beams, one above and one below, between which the warp threads are stretched.

and the nirim. The warp threads are passed over reeds called nirim that lie parallel to the loom's beams: half of the threads (the even ones) over one reed, and the other half (the odd ones) over a second reed. When one nir is raised, all the threads attached to it rise, and thus an opening is made for passing the weft thread.
and the kiros. A kind of comb used for pressing the weft threads that were threaded between the warp threads.

and the thread they passed over the purple. A thread used for embroidering the purple (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 21:1): a thread is sewn into the fabric to mark where the purple should be embroidered, and afterward it is removed from the weave. Some explain that it is a thread with which the purple embroidery is covered so it will not get dirty, and at the end of the work it is removed (Rash there).

and the ayrah which he does not intend to return. After passing the warp thread through the weft, part of the warp thread remains outside the fabric. If he intends not to continue passing that thread between the weft threads but to cut it and use a new thread, the end of the thread outside the weaving is pure.
but one who touches the nefesh of the loom. The weft threads that were inserted into the warp weave but not yet pressed to the fabric but slightly distant from it.
and the standing warp. The warp threads stretched between the beams.
and the doubled thread they passed over the purple. A thread embroidered in the fabric together with the purple threads.

one who touches the wool on the imah. The imah is a bobbin (see the explanation above 10:4).
