If it became impure and one touched the wool thread on it, he does not become impure, since the thread is not considered a connection to the imah (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 21:1; and Rash explained that the imah is the stick on which the wool for spinning sits - see above 10:14).
and the needle. A needle with which threads are embroidered in a garment (see Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 21:1), and if one touched the thread, he does not become impure from the needle.
on the whorl. A kind of ball on which a skein of wool thread is wound.

before he unravels it etc.. If the thread is wound around the spool so that it covers it completely, it is considered connected to the spool, and one who touches the thread becomes impure. If a little of the thread remains and it does not cover the whole spool, the thread is not considered connected to the spool.
a thread that he threaded onto a needle. He passed it through the eye of the needle.
even if it is tied on both sides. Even if he tied the two ends of the thread so that the thread cannot come out of the needle.
it is not a connection. Because he will eventually sew the thread into the garment and detach it from the needle.
a thread that extends from the garment, even a hundred cubits, is all a connection. Because it was already part of the garment.

a rope tied to a ceramic vessel. So it reads in the manuscripts, but it seems that one should read "to a net", meaning a fishing net made of ropes (Chiddushei HaRambam, Kelim, Tosefta Bava Metzia 9:4; Sidrei Taharot 188a; R. Y. Kafah).

even a hundred cubits, all of it is a connection. Because the whole rope is destined to be woven into the net (Chiddushei HaRambam, ibid.). Some explain that this refers to a rope with which the net is hauled up from the water, and all of it is considered a handle for the net because the entire length of the rope is needed (Tosefta Kelim p. 63; see also Chiddushei HaRambam).
he tied another rope to it. To the rope that is tied to the net.

from the knot inward is a connection; from the knot outward is not a connection. The first rope is considered connected to the net, and the second rope tied to it is not a connection (Sidrei Taharot, ibid.). It is possible to explain that "from the knot outward" means that not only is the second rope not a connection, but also the end of the first rope that hangs beyond the knot is not considered a connection (compare below 21:6).
what is their measure. To be considered connected to a garment with regard to impurity.
head wraps. A turban in which the head is wrapped.
a scarf. A light scarf.
a woman's head covering. A women's head kerchief (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 29:1).
a tunic that is torn from top to bottom and, after it is put on, is gathered with loops. A garment open along its entire length that is closed with loops.
the sagos. Thick woolen fabric. [Note: in several manuscripts the reading is "the sagum".]
and the radid. A thin scarf.
and everything in excess of these measures. The part beyond the measure.
the threads of the kufach. The fringe threads of the kerchief.
and the belts woven from hair. A girth with which an animal is girded, made of animal hair.
and the pundah that a person wears next to his skin. A garment that absorbs sweat, like an undershirt.
their threads, of any length. Of any length, they are considered connected to the garment.
a plumb weight that became impure. A weight attached to a balance.
and the plumb weight of carpenters. A weight attached to a string, which carpenters use to check whether wooden beams stand straight.
and that of builders. With which builders check that a wall of a building is straight.

and anything beyond these measures, even if he wants to keep it, is pure. Because this is not found at all, and his intention is nullified. (But for the utensils listed above, 20:12, it is common that sometimes long handles are needed, and therefore one who wants to keep them has not nullified his intention. Hon Ashir, Kelim 29:3.)
and that of painters. Those who paint on the walls of a house.

a scale string. The string that the weigher holds in his hand and from which the scale hangs. For goods sold in heavy weights a long string is used, and for goods sold in small weights a short string is used (see Hilchot Genevah 8:8-11).
goldsmiths. Sellers of gold.
and that of a pales. A type of balance (perhaps this refers to the scale of a money changer with which he weighs coins; see R. Yosef Migash, Bava Batra 89a).
its beam. The beam of the balance.
and its strings. The strings that descend from the beam and from which the pans of the scale hang.
ingots of metals. Metal ores.
wool sellers. Sellers of wool.

the rope with which beds are laced etc.. The bed is made of a wooden frame, and ropes were tied between the beams of the frame, on which the bedding was placed. The space between one rope and the next is called a "bayit" (cell).
and one who touches the rope from the knot inward. Toward the part that has already been laced (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 19:1).
from the knot outward. The end of the rope that extends beyond the knot.
for even if he cuts it off, the knot does not come undone. Even if he cuts off the remainder of the rope, the knot will not open.
a rope that extends from the bed. A rope that is tied to the finished bed.
up to four handbreadths. If the rope is up to four handbreadths long.
one who touches it is pure, as it is not among the needs of the bed. Because such a rope has no use.
because beds are hung by it. When the bed is lowered from floor to floor or from the roof to the house, they hold the rope and lower the bed down.
from ten outward is pure. The part longer than ten handbreadths is pure (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 19:2).
which is wrapped around the bed to hold its parts together. Like a wide belt around the frame of the bed in order to strengthen it.
a girth for a donkey. To fasten the saddle cloth to the donkey.
a bed that was impure with midras impurity. That a zav pressed upon (see Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 7:1).

from ten outward it is like contact with midras. Beyond ten, the mattress is not among the needs of the bed and is considered a separate vessel, and its impurity is that of one who touched a midras, which is a first-degree impurity.

if a zav pressed upon the projecting mattress etc.. With midras impurity, only utensils made for lying or sitting and the like become impure, and they become impure even when there is a separation between them and the zav who is on them. The part of the mattress within ten handbreadths is considered part of the bed, so when the zav presses on it, the mattress becomes impure and the bed becomes impure with it. But the part of the mattress outside ten handbreadths is not considered a vessel made for lying, so if the zav pressed on it without touching, it does not become impure at all (see Mishnah Acharonah, Kelim 19:4; Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 6:5).

in what case does this apply to midras etc.. With other impurities, all utensils become impure, not only a vessel made for lying, so the mattress becomes impure along its entire length, and it makes the bed impure because it is connected to it (Tosefta Kelim, Bava Metzia 9:6).

if it was impure with seven-day impurity. That it became impure through a corpse and needs seven days to become pure. (This speaks of a bed that touched utensils that touched a corpse; if the bed itself had touched a corpse, then a utensil touching it would also have seven-day impurity. Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 19:5; Hilchot Tumat Met 5:4.)
the mattress is impure with impurity until evening. That it has the law of one who touched a primary source of impurity and became a first-degree impurity; he immerses it and it is pure by evening.
if it was impure with impurity until evening. That the bed became impure from a primary source of impurity such as a creeping animal or a carcass, and it is itself a derivative of impurity.
the mattress is pure. Because a derivative of impurity does not make utensils impure (Hilchot Tumat Met 5:7).

a bed to which a mattress was wrapped, and a corpse touched them etc.. In this case the bed and the mattress are like one vessel, and both became impure through the corpse or the creeping animal, and therefore even when they are separated they remain in their impurity.
a leg. The leg of the bed.
that was impure with midras impurity. That a zav pressed upon it before he attached it to the bed.
and if he sprinkled on the bed. With the waters of the purification offering, to purify them from corpse impurity.
the leg is purified along with it. Even if the waters of the purification offering did not touch it, since the bed and the leg are considered one body for both impurity and purification.
as we have explained. Hilchot Tumat Met 5:7.
and so the law for the tooth of a hoe. The metal part of the hoe, which is detached and attached to the handle.
what is the measure of a garment to become impure. This speaks here of pieces of cloth torn from a garment (as explained later in the halakhah), and they become impure when they are fit for some use.

three handbreadths by three handbreadths for midras. At this measure it is fit to sit on. Midras is the impurity that a utensil receives because a zav sat, lay or rode on it (see Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 7:1).
precise. Measured exactly.
with the fringe. The threads that project from the edges of the garment.
for corpse impurity or other impurities. At this measure it is fit for various uses, such as serving as a patch for a garment, but not for midras.
from oral tradition. The tradition of the Sages in the interpretation of the verses.
in torn pieces that come from garments. A garment that was torn and a piece of cloth of a certain size remains from it.
but one who weaves a garment on its own, of any size. A complete garment, such as a belt that is less than three finger-breadths wide.

for only that which is fit for midras receives it. That which is made to sit or lie on, and a garment smaller than three by three handbreadths is not fit for this. (See below 23:3, that there are cases where it receives midras impurity even at less than this.)
and blankets. Sheets and covers.

do not receive impurity until the tear is three handbreadths by three handbreadths. Because a piece of very thick or very thin cloth is not fit for use at a small size, until it has the measure of three handbreadths.
a ribbon. A band, a cord.
to tie the wool with it. The bundles of wool that stand for sale.
it is pure. Because it is not considered a vessel but serves as a thread and rope (Commentary to the Mishnah, Eduyot 3:4).
the sling. With which stones are shot.
its finger loop. A loop at the end of the sling into which one puts the finger when whirling the sling.
pure. Because one cannot shoot with the sling and it has lost its function.
the pakia end. The other end of the sling, which is held in the hand during the whirling and released when the stone is shot.
it is still in its impurity. Because one can still use the sling in this way.
and the net. A net with large holes.
receives impurity because of the zuto. The part at the bottom of the net that is woven densely.
because the holes of that netting are very fine and it is like a garment. The holes in the zuto of the net are very small, and it has the law of a garment.
one who makes a garment from a net is pure. The net is not fit for a garment because it has large holes and the flesh is visible through them.
the strainer. A sieve.
if it has three by three it receives impurity. Like the law of garment remnants.
worn out. It became worn.
if it still serves in the manner of its original function it is impure. If it still serves for straining wine.
and if not it is pure. Like the law of broken vessels, and it does not have the law of a garment, whose measure is three by three (Aruch HaShulchan 224:16).
the decorated book covers. Covers that wrap Torah scrolls, which are dyed or embroidered.
because they are not used by people. See above 4:1.
and those that are not decorated become impure with other impurities. Because they serve for other tasks.
except for midras impurity. For with midras impurity only things specifically for lying and sitting become impure, but not utensils intended for another task.
because they say to him, "Get up and let us do our work". The cloth is intended for work and not for sitting, and if the zav sat on it, they would tell him to get up so they can use the cloth.
as we have explained regarding the impurity of lying and sitting. Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 7:8.
and the porters' pad. A cushion that porters place on their shoulders as padding.
becomes impure with midras. Because the porter sits on it when he rests from his work (Tiferet Yisrael, Kelim 28:9), and it was originally made for that as well.
and a wine strainer does not become impure with midras. Because people are not accustomed to sit on it because of the lees that soil the clothes (Rash and Tiferet Yisrael, ibid.).
a garment that he designated for designs. From the start of its making the garment was not meant for wearing but to make a design on it, which embroiderers would copy and learn from.
does not receive impurity. Because it is not among the things people use (below 27:12).
if he nullified his intention, it receives impurity. For all utensils become subject to impurity through intention (above 8:10).
to cover walls and pillars, they do not receive impurity. Because they are not used by people (Chiddushei HaRambam, Kelim, Bava Metzia 5:9).
a tunic made like a net. Like netting through which the flesh is visible.
to play with it, to drink strong drink. At entertainment shows that involve immodesty (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 28:9).
does not receive impurity. Because it is not fit for wearing.
a kufach. A head wrap.
that he placed over a book. To serve as a book cover.
it is pure from receiving midras impurity but becomes impure with corpse impurity and other impurities. Like the law of undecorated book covers (above halakhah 6).
one who makes a poultice. A bandage: he puts a substance such as oil or wax on the cloth and places it on the skin for healing.
pure. Because they get soiled and spoiled.
he made a plaster upon them. A bandage of non-fatty materials such as flour and crushed figs (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 28:3).
from when does a garment receive impurity. When one prepares pieces of cloth or a garment without a particular shape, such as a tallit.

once he has woven three finger-breadths by three finger-breadths in it. Even though its work is not finished (for a complete garment receives impurity even when smaller than three by three, as above halakhah 1).
those woven with a needle. Sewn.
and an anpalya. A sock.

do not receive impurity until their work is finished. For in ordinary woven fabric people use various sizes as needed, and the smallest size that has significance is three by three. But something that is knitted is intended for the specific use for which it was knitted.
those made on a needle. Utensils whose manufacture includes weaving with a needle.

once he has made in them a receptacle, their work is finished and they receive impurity. Although the manner of their making is similar to garments, they do not have the law of a garment regarding completion of work, but receive impurity when a receptacle is made in them, like other utensils (above 5:1).
a hairnet. A kerchief.
its mouth. The edge of the hairnet, which is tied around the head.
its crown. The middle of the hairnet, the part placed on the top of the head.
and its shavis. An ornament made of gold or gold-threaded cloth attached to the hairnet; it receives impurity as an ornament even when it is not attached to the hairnet.
and its threads. Threads that come out of the hairnet with which it is tied to the head.
pure. Because it is not fit for wearing.
a tunic of cloth. Made of spun and woven fabric.
felt. Fabric that is not spun and woven, made of compressed fibers.
once he opens its mouth. The opening through which the head and neck are inserted.
for an adult according to his size and for a child according to his size. According to the size of the tunic, so as to fit the person for whose measure the tunic was sewn.

once it wears out and no longer serves in the manner of its original function. For wearing; and even though it has three by three and is fit to receive impurity as torn pieces of garments, it is purified from the impurity that was on it (Chazon Ish, Kelim 30:8, 32:11).
if most of it remains from above it is still in its impurity. Because the shoulders hold it and it can be worn.
most of it from below is pure. Because it cannot be worn (compare above 11:10).
and if it was torn from its mouth opening. The neck opening.
one who makes a belt from the side of a garment. He cut a strip from the edge of the garment to make a belt from it.
until he hems its edges. Until he folds it slightly and sews the side that was cut from the garment so that the threads do not stick out.

he made it from the middle of the garment and from the middle of the sheet. He cut the strip from the middle of the garment, and there are threads protruding from both sides of the belt because it is cut on both sides.
does not receive impurity until he hems its second side. Until he sews both sides of the strip.
a belt whose sides wore away while its middle is intact is impure. Even though the sides have unraveled it remains in its impurity until it unravels completely.
a border. A kind of small belt that is sewn onto the edge of a garment.
and he prepared it to gird his loins with it, it receives impurity. Even without sewing.
a poor person's tallit that has worn out. That has become worn, and a poor person does not throw away his clothes even when they are worn.

even though it does not have three by three that is sound. That it does not have three by three finger-breadths continuous without a tear (Chiddushei HaRambam, Kelim, Bava Batra 6:3); some explain that it does not have three by three finger-breadths of strong cloth (Aruch HaShulchan 226:3).
and so too other clothes of the poor. But worn clothes of the wealthy do not receive impurity, because they do not use them (ibid. 226:5).
patches. Pieces of worn garments.

that do not have three handbreadths by three handbreadths do not receive impurity etc.. And pieces of a whole garment receive impurity even without preparation, as explained above halakhah 1 (Chazon Ish, Kelim 28:17; see Mishnah Acharonah, Kelim 28:2, who distinguishes between the halakhot in a different way).
to plug the bathhouse with it. To seal cracks in the walls of the bathhouse so that the steam does not escape and it does not cool.
and to take hold of the pot with it. To grasp the pot when it is hot.
and to wipe the millstones with it. From the dust and the remains of flour.
if he threw it onto the rubbish heap it does not receive impurity. Because he completely nullified it (as explained below, halakhah 26).

if he hung it on his garment... it is as if he placed it among his clothes and it is still important to him. Even though he prepared it for an unimportant use, the place of the cloth shows that he intends to keep it and has not yet nullified it.

if it was sound enough to tie in it a quarter-kab of coarse salt. If the cloth is whole (sound) and also strong enough that one can tie in it a quarter-kab (about 300 cc) of coarse salt, which tears a cloth more than fine salt does (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 27:11).
but if it was in the house. That he did not throw it onto the rubbish heap, showing that he regards it as a garment.
if it was sound, even though he cannot tie salt in it. That it was whole but weak and tore because of the salt.
or that he could tie salt and it was not sound. That the cloth is strong and can tie salt but it is not whole and has tears in it.
three by three that was torn but the tears were not separated. They were not torn along their entire length and the parts are still connected to each other.
he puts it on the chair, and when he sits on it his flesh touches the chair, it is pure. From midras, as it cannot be used for sitting (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 27:12).
that wore out. It became worn, weakened.
or a knot was found in it. In one of the threads.
or two threads that are adjacent. That one weft thread is missing and the weft threads on either side of it stuck together.
it is pure. Because in such a small piece even a small defect makes it lose its importance (Chazon Ish, Kelim 33:2).
except for those of purple and good crimson. Wool dyed in precious colors.
that he put into a ball. As stuffing.
or that he made into a ball. He filled it with fluff and sewed it around.
pure. Because he nullified its importance and does not intend to restore it.
but three handbreadths by three handbreadths that he put into a ball remains as it was. Because the cloth is kept inside the ball and perhaps he will take it out and use it (Rash, Kelim 28:1).
and it becomes impure with midras. If the zav sat on the ball.
for the seam reduces it below three by three. For he places the edges of the cloth one on the other and sews, and so the area of the cloth is reduced.
and a mat is not included among the utensils mentioned in the Torah. Because it is a wooden utensil that has no receptacle (Hilchot Mikva'ot 1:4).

and nevertheless it becomes impure with midras by Torah law, for the verse included "every bed". As it says: "Every bed on which the zav lies shall be impure" (Leviticus 15:4), from which we learn that anything fit for lying becomes impure (and see Hilchot Mikva'ot there: because its impurity is not stated explicitly but learned from an amplification, it has no purification in a mikveh, only by tearing).

and likewise it becomes impure with corpse impurity and other impurities by rabbinic law, like all flat wooden utensils, as we have explained. Even when the mat is not fit for midras, it becomes impure by rabbinic law if it serves people and utensils, like the law of flat wooden utensils, as explained above 4:1.

and this is a great principle: anything that becomes impure with midras becomes impure with other impurities. When the mat is fit for midras it receives impurity from other impurities by rabbinic law even when it does not serve people and utensils (Mikdash David, Taharot 52).
we have already explained. Above 22:1.
sackcloth. Weaving or plaiting from animal hair (above 1:12).

it is entirely pure. It does not receive impurity at all. These measures apply to simple sheets. But if he made from them a special vessel meant for midras, they receive impurity even at less than these measures (see below 24:4, and see also later in the halakhah).
but one who cuts intentionally. Because he wants a small piece.
a handbreadth by a handbreadth for sitting. To sit on the piece that he cut.
it is impure at any size. At any measure greater than three by three finger-breadths.

one who joins two handbreadths from the garment and one handbreadth from the sackcloth... it is pure from midras. Because the completion of the measure of three by three, at which the garment becomes impure, was made by the sackcloth, which becomes impure only at four by four handbreadths.

but if he joined five handbreadths from the mat and one from the leather... it is impure with midras. Because the completion of the measure of six by six handbreadths, at which the mat becomes impure, was made by the leather, which becomes impure already at five handbreadths.
anyone who completes his measure with something stricter than it. That receives impurity at a smaller measure.
he completed it with the more lenient. With something that receives impurity at a larger measure.
until he trims them. He cuts their edges and straightens them.

and afterwards they are like a mat. If he trimmed them without a specific purpose, they have the law of a mat, whose measure for midras is six by six handbreadths. If he trimmed them intentionally to sit on them, they become impure even at a handbreadth by a handbreadth, as explained above halakhah 3 (Sidrei Taharot, Kelim 249a).
a child's tunic. A garment of an infant.
does not become impure with midras until it has the measure of three handbreadths by three handbreadths. Even though it is a complete garment, because it is not fit for midras (above 22:1).
and it is measured folded as it was made. Its area is measured as sewn, and we do not say that he should cut the seams and flatten the cloth and then measure.
and the pocket of a pundah. An undershirt or a wide belt worn tight against the body.
and a patch that he patched onto the border. A piece that he sewed onto the edge of the garment.
if flat it is measured flat, and if folded it is measured folded. If he sewed the piece on flat, all of it is measured; if he folded it and sewed it, the folded area is measured as it is.
the whole garment is midras. And it is a primary source of impurity, since all of it is connected to the three by three that became impure.
one thread was removed from its beginning. From the part of the garment that he wove first and that became impure.
it is pure from midras. For the garment that he wove first is now less than three by three.
but it is impure by contact with midras. And it is a first-degree impurity, since for contact impurity a measure of three finger-breadths suffices, as with all impurities.

one thread was removed from its beginning and afterwards he completed the whole garment, the whole garment is impure by contact with midras. Since the garment that fell short of three by three was purified from midras, but it is regarded as if it had touched it itself, and is impure by contact with midras.
the whole garment is impure with corpse impurity. And it is a primary source of impurity.
impure by contact with a corpse-impure item. A first-degree impurity.
a patch that is midras. That became impure with midras, and it is a primary source of impurity that makes utensils impure.
and he patched it onto a basket. He sewed it onto a wooden basket.

the whole became first-degree impurity. The basket became impure from contact with the patch and became first-degree impurity, and the patch itself is nullified from being impure with midras because it is a patch to the basket or the leather and secondary to them.
and the patch is pure, for once he patched it on and separated it, it was nullified. As if he had torn and ruined it, and it is nullified from being considered a garment.

he patched it onto a garment or a sack, the whole became midras. The patch is not nullified to a garment or sack because they too are of the type of woven fabric (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 28:6), and they have the law of a garment that became impure with midras and he added to it, so all of it is impure with midras (above halakhah 7).
in the shape of a gam. In the shape of the Greek letter gamma, whose form is: Γ.
he sewed it from two sides opposite each other, it is a connection. From two parallel sides, since with such sewing the patch is attached to the garment.
three by three that became impure with midras and afterwards was divided. And in the two parts there is no measure of three by three.

and these torn pieces have no impurity at all. Because by tearing the garment he nullifies it and purifies it of its impurity. (But above halakhah 7, when one thread is missing, the garment is not completely nullified but only falls short of the measure fit to receive midras, and therefore it is impure by contact with midras. Meiri.)

but a garment that became impure with midras and from which he tore three finger-breadths by three finger-breadths. And a measure of three by three remains in the garment, it is still impure with midras and makes impure by contact the piece that was separated from the garment.
and afterwards he made it a curtain, it is pure from midras. It is purified from the midras impurity it had, since a curtain is not meant for lying and does not become impure with midras.
a tallit that is midras and he immersed it. The tallit is not completely purified until the night after immersion, called "ha'erev shemesh" (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumah 10:1).
before its sun set, he began to tear a tear from it. He does not want to wait until night, but to purify it immediately by tearing.
even though a maafortet-size piece still remains of it that was not torn. That a piece the size of a kerchief that is fit to become impure remains of the garment.
for he is tearing continuously. For he will eventually tear the whole tallit, and so it is pure already from the moment he tore most of it.

since he did not spare it from immersion, he will not spare tearing all of it. We do not worry that he might not tear the whole tallit, since he immersed it in water for purification and did not worry about spoiling the tallit.
these hides become impure with midras. Those made for lying or sitting.
and a hide that is placed on a donkey under the load. Because sometimes people lie on it (Melechet Shlomo, Kelim 26:5).
and a hide that is placed on a cradle under a child. Placed in the infant's cradle so that he does not wet the bedding beneath him.
the donkey driver. One who transports loads on donkeys.
and the hide that a flax beater wears. One who beats or combs flax fibers to separate them girds himself with a hide so that the flax fibers do not stick to his clothes (Rash, Kelim 26:5).
when he carries a load. While carrying a burden, so that the load does not hurt him (ibid.).
when he lances boils. While piercing pus-filled wounds, so that his clothes do not get soiled (ibid.).
a child's heart hide. An infant's apron.
and a hide in which a garment is wrapped. In which one wraps a garment.
and a hide sewn like a box. A kind of leather case in which clothes are placed.
until they have the measure of five handbreadths by five handbreadths. See also above 23:3.
and these are hides that do not become impure with midras. Because people are not accustomed to sit on them (see Tiferet Yisrael, Kelim 26:5).
a hide that he made as a covering for utensils is entirely pure. For the covering of utensils does not receive impurity (above 4:4).
he made it a covering for a weight. To protect it from being damaged and losing weight.

it receives other impurities because it was made for receiving, and it does not become impure with midras. For when weighing with the weight, the weight must be exact, and so they take it out of the leather covering, so the leather is like a receptacle for the weight (Rambam LeAm).
a hide that he made for his heel and his hoof. To wrap around his heel or the sole of his foot, and it is not a complete shoe (Chiddushei HaRambam, Kelim, Bava Batra 4:4).

if it covers most of the foot, it becomes impure. If the hide covers most of the foot it becomes impure with midras. And although it was explained above halakhah 2 that a hide without five by five does not become impure with midras, and an ordinary foot has no such measure, this rule applies only to a plain hide that has no shape of a vessel (Chiddushei HaRambam, ibid.; Chazon Ish, Kelim 30:19).
a shoe on the form... as we have explained. Above 7:1.
that which is fit to become impure with midras. Fit to sit or lie on.
and it is not lacking work. It is ready for the use he intends, and there is no need to process it or cut it to measure and the like.
intention makes it impure. Prepares it to receive impurity.
with which the saddle is covered because of dust. They cover the saddle with it so that it does not get dirty.
for intention is effective for it even though its work was not finished. Because it is made only for covering and they are not particular about finishing its work or its exact measure.

intention does not make them impure until he performs an act on them and prepares them for midras. Hides standing for sale do not become impure since they are for the needs of customers, and until the buyer does something to them their work is not finished. And even if the tanner thought to use them as they are, his intention is not effective since he may change his mind and sell them (Kesef Mishneh).

as it is said, "and he who touches his bed". Only one who touches the bed of the zav makes impure; hence a bed does not become impure with midras and become a primary source of impurity that makes a person impure unless it is a bed belonging to the zav (Maggid Mishneh; see Piskim VeShitot).
he robbed a bed and pressed upon it without touching. For example, there was a separation between the zav and the midras.

pure. But if the zav touched it while pressing, the bed became impure by the zav's contact and became first-degree impurity (and makes food and drink impure). For the verse excluded only midras impurity and not contact impurity.

and if the owners gave up hope, it is impure. Because through giving up hope the hide no longer belongs to the owners for this purpose (Lechem Mishneh, Hilchot Gezelah 2:1), and with an ordinary robber we assume the owners have not given up hope, since they know who the robber is and hope to sue him and recover the stolen item from him.

therefore a thief who stole a hide and thought of it for lying etc.. The rule is that a utensil becomes subject to impurity only through the intention of its owners (below 25:11), and the intention of another is effective only after the owner has given up hope. Therefore in the case of a thief, where we assume the owner gave up hope, his intention is effective; in the case of a robber, where we assume the owner did not give up hope, his intention is not effective, unless it is known that the owner gave up hope (Maggid Mishneh).
and he began to tear it into strips. Which are thin and do not become impure with midras.
it remains in its impurity until he reduces it to less than five handbreadths. Which is the measure of a hide for midras (above halakhah 2).
the flat one. A flat hide.
into a receptacle. A container.

if he changed it from flat to a receptacle and from a receptacle to flat, it is pure. For a new vessel was made, as if the old vessel had been torn and was purified of its impurity (Chiddushei HaRambam, Kelim, Bava Batra 6:1).

but with a garment everything is impure. Because he can undo the seams and return the garment to its former shape, the change made in it is not considered permanent and it is not like a new vessel. But leather is harder than cloth and takes on the shape of the new vessel made from it, and it takes great effort to restore it (Chiddushei HaRambam, ibid.; see another reason in Aruch HaShulchan 228:17).
a waterskin. A container for liquids.
that he made into a rug. He tore it and spread it flat to sit on it.
and a rug that he made into a waterskin. By sewing.
pure. Because he changed it from flat to receptacle or the reverse.
a bag. A knapsack, a satchel.

a waterskin... and he made it a bag, or a bag that he made a waterskin, they are midras as they were. Because both are receptacles, and changing from receptacle to receptacle remains impure (Tosafot Yom Tov, Kelim 28:5; Chiddushei HaRambam, Kelim, Bava Batra 6:1; but see the note of R. Saul Lieberman on Chiddushei HaRambam there).
a cushion of cloth. Made of fabric.
they are midras as they were. Even though he changed the cloth from flat to receptacle or the reverse, since a garment remains impure even when its shape is changed (above halakhah 9).
utensils whose main making was for receiving and for lying alike. That from the outset they were made both for holding and for lying.
and the marzufin. Large sacks for storing goods.
if they were torn. They were torn and the stuffing falls out of them.

they become impure with midras, for they are still fit for midras. Although the rule is that whatever becomes impure with midras becomes impure with other impurities (above 23:1), a utensil that was torn and spoiled has lost the status of a vessel and does not become impure with other impurities (Tosafot Yom Tov, Kelim 24:4; Chiddushei Maharich, Kelim 20:1; see Aruch HaShulchan 228:23).
and what is their measure so that they are fit for midras. That they are large enough to be fit to sit on.
and the kalaster with which barley is hung on the animal's head. A bag that is filled with barley so that the animal eats from it.
and the keritit with which water is poured. A flask.

all flat wooden utensils made for sitting, lying or riding become impure with midras. Although flat wooden utensils do not receive impurity, when they are fit for sitting or lying they become impure with midras by Torah law (and consequently they also become impure with other impurities by rabbinic law, as above 23:1).

the bed, the pillow and the cushion of a dead person. Made for the dead person. Although a dead person has no bed or seat (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 23:4; see below 27:13), they are impure with midras because the mourners sit on them (Tosefta Kelim, Bava Batra 2:8).
and a birthing stool for a woman in labor. A chair for a woman in labor to sit on during childbirth.

and the chair of a launderer on which he presses the garments. A press with which the launderer smooths garments, and it is impure with midras because the launderer sits on it with the garments inside to press them and smooth them (Kesef Mishneh).
even if it is not a handbreadth high. For it is fit for a child (compare below 26:2).
an iron chair made for the privy. A toilet seat.
he separated the leather... the leather becomes impure with midras. For the leather is fit for sitting on its own.
and the iron becomes impure with other impurities but not with midras. For one does not sit on the iron without the leather covering.
a reed trasqal. The meaning of the word trasqal here is a woven three-legged chair (see Aruch HaShalem, entry "trasqal").
covered with leather. To make it comfortable to sit on.
entirely pure. It does not receive impurity at all.
for it has become like broken vessels. For it is not fit for sitting because it is rough.
the benches in the bathhouse. Whose seats are made of marble.

the two legs of a wooden bench become impure with midras. Although the marble seat does not receive impurity, like the law of stone vessels (above 1:6), the wooden legs are made for midras and receive impurity.
if one was of wood and one of marble, it does not receive impurity. For the entire bench is considered a stone vessel (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 22:10).

boards in the bathhouse that he heated. The bathhouse room was heated by a furnace that was stoked beneath the floor of the room. The hot air from the furnace heated the water on the bathhouse floor, and the air of the room was warmed by the steam. So that one could walk on the floor without being burned, boards were placed on it and the bathers stood on them. They do not receive impurity, since they are not meant for sitting like benches but to separate between the hot floor and the feet of the bathers (Perush Sefarai, Kelim 22:10).
rags. Small pieces of cloth.
even though he prepared them for sitting. That he filled the basket in order to sit on it.
for they are not fit for sitting. Because the rags and straw come out through the mouth of the basket.
and if he laced them etc.. He made a net over the mouth of the basket of reed or thread.
the beam of the olive press. Used for pressing olives.

because they say to him, "Get up and let us do our work". The beam is meant for pressing and not for sitting, and if he sat on the chair they would tell him to get up so that they can use the beam for pressing.
but if he fixed the chair into the beam of the olive press etc.. In this case the chair is considered a separate vessel from the beam.
and likewise if he fixed the chair into a large beam. In an ordinary beam not specific to the olive press, if he fixed a chair in it, it is considered a vessel in itself.

he made the end of the large beam a chair. If he made the end of the beam itself into a chair, the place of the chair becomes impure, because it is not designated for work like the beam of the olive press, and we do not say to him, "Get up and let us do our work."
in a trough. A large basin meant for kneading.

it is pure. Some explain that the chair does receive impurity but is not a connection to the trough, and if the trough became impure the chair does not become impure (Kesef Mishneh). Others explain that the chair is entirely pure because fixing it in the trough nullifies it from serving for sitting, and it has the law of a broken vessel (Tosafot Yom Tov, Kelim 22:4).
part of the beam. The end of the beam.
ends of poles. Long beams.
pure. Because they were not specially prepared for that.
a log of a palm tree. A block of palm wood (this is the language of the Tosefta Kelim, Bava Batra 2:1, and the same applies to other woods, as explained here).
that he combed and dyed red. He dyed it with kinds of red dye.
and made it a facing for the gate and the like. He fixed it in the gate for decoration.
if he hollowed them intentionally. In order to sit on them.
if he thought of them. To use them as a seat.
only the intention of owners. See above 24:7.
who are possessed of understanding. See above 2:1.
a lump. A clump.
of leaven. Sour dough of flour and water used to make dough rise.
for it is used for the uses of wood. He uses it as if it were wood, and therefore it is no longer considered food.
chelef. Sand reed.
because it is not fit for midras. Because it is not comfortable for lying.
he made it for shade. For shade.

a mat on which he made reeds along its length is impure with midras. Although it is not usual to place reeds along the length of a mat but along its width, if he placed the reeds lengthwise and left room for lying between the reeds, it receives impurity (Tiferet Yisrael, Kelim 20:7).
he made them in the shape of a gam, it is pure. He placed reeds in the shape of the Greek letter gamma, Γ, and one cannot lie either along the mat or across it.

it was split across its width. The reeds were usually placed across the width of the mat to strengthen it, and when it was split across its width the reeds on it broke (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 20:7).
it still receives impurity. For the breaking of the reeds alone does not nullify the mat if it still has the measure for midras, as explained shortly.

three maadanim of six handbreadths. They would tie the ends of the straw from which the mat is made so that it would not come apart, making one knot every two handbreadths. If a width of six handbreadths remains in the mat with three knots in it, it still receives impurity, at the measure of a mat that became impure with midras (above 23:3).
and likewise if he untied the ends of the maadanim it is pure. Because it is about to come apart.
and let it be trimmed. The protruding ends will be cut.
as we have explained. Above 5:1.
and it receives other impurities. Because it has a receptacle.
and whose opening is at its side is impure with midras and other impurities. Because it is also fit for sitting.
a child's cart. On which the infant leans when learning to walk (Tosafot Beitzah 23b).
a plasterers' sandal. A wooden clog that protects the plasterers' feet from being burned by lime.
an amputee's peg that has a receptacle of soft cloths. A wooden leg that has a hollow with soft cloths in which to rest the shin.

and these are impure because of the merkav. Because they are made to ride on. The merkav is a primary source of impurity like the bed and the seat, except that, unlike them, one who touches a merkav does not make clothes and utensils impure at the time of contact (see Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 6:2).
a mardaat. A kind of rug placed beneath the saddle.
and the horse's tapeitan. A saddle.
and the camel's cushion. A round seat made of cloth (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 23:2).
a she-camel. A female camel.
the boards placed on the back of the donkey and then the load is placed on them are pure. They have the law of flat wooden utensils because one does not ride on them.
he fixed it and did not build on top of it. He attached it to the wall with nails and did not place stones and earth on it.

or he built on top of it and did not fix it. He placed stones on it but did not fix it with nails, so it can be removed; and the zav makes the vessel impure when he sits on the stone above it, because the zav makes bed and seat impure even when something intervenes between them (Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 7:1).
he fixed it with nails and built on it, it is pure. Because the vessel became part of the wall and does not receive impurity.
a mat. See above 23:1.
that he placed over the beams. To serve as a ceiling.
he fixed it and did not put the maazevah on it. The earth and lime placed on the boards of the ceiling.
a bench. That stands on two wide legs.
if one of its ends was removed it is still fit for midras. Perhaps because it can be leaned against the wall and sat upon (compare below halakhah 13).

and if it has a height of a handbreadth it becomes impure with midras. Because it is fit to sit on; but at less than a handbreadth it is considered as if he were sitting on the ground (Kesef Mishneh).
a bride's chair. A chair inlaid with ivory and precious woods.
whose inlays were removed is pure. Because it is no longer used, and it is like a broken vessel (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 22:4).
if its inlays did not protrude. If the inlays do not protrude outward but are set into recesses in the chair.

it is still fit for midras, for it is its way to tilt it on its side and sit on it. Even when the inlays were in place it could be tilted on its side and sat upon, and so it was not nullified from its use when the inlays were removed. But when the inlays protrude outward it cannot be tilted and is used only when standing in its normal way, so when the inlays were removed its use was nullified.

a chair whose inlays were removed etc.. The rule is that when a chair is not fit for sitting it becomes pure. From the Commentary to the Mishnah (Kelim 22:6) it appears that the inlays discussed here surround the chair, and when two of them were removed it is not fit for sitting; but the exact form of the inlays is not known to us. (In the view of the Rash the inlays are three boards from which the seat of the chair is built.)

a shidah. A cabinet built of two compartments one on top of the other, the compartments open to the side, with a top surface that can be sat upon (see Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 22:8; Sidrei Taharot, Kelim 202b).
whose upper one was removed. The top of the upper compartment.
it is impure because of the lower one, which is fit for midras. Because one can sit on the top of the lower compartment.
the lower one was removed. The top of the lower compartment.
the upper and the lower were removed. And only the side walls of the cabinet and the floor of the lower compartment remained.
the boards are pure. Because one cannot sit on them or use them as receptacles.
a chest that was breached on its side. It broke so that a hole formed in the wall of the chest from the side.

it becomes impure with midras as with other impurities. It became impure with midras because it is fit for sitting, and with other impurities because a chest open on its side is still considered a receptacle.
it was breached from above. If it was not broken from the side but the lid of the chest was broken from above so that it is open upward and cannot be sat upon.
and it becomes impure with other impurities, for it still receives. Since it has four walls and is a receptacle for all purposes (compare above 25:15).
it was breached from below. The bottom of the chest was broken.
and the compartments. Drawers, cells.
a mashpelet. A large basket for taking manure out to the fields.
a trough. A basin.
in which builders mix plaster. They mix gypsum and water in it.
he left it in the rains until it swelled. The wood swells from the water.
he again left it in the east wind. The east wind, and the trough dried and the crack opened again.
and is pure from other impurities. It does not receive impurity except midras, because it ceased to be a vessel (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 20:2).
until he trims. He cuts the edges of the trough and straightens them for sitting.
for intention is not effective for a large trough that was breached until he performs an act on it. Because of its size it is not fit for sitting (Tiferet Yisrael, Kelim 20:4).
even if he fixed it in the wall it is impure with all impurities. For fixing it in the wall does not change the use of the trough (compare above 11:24).

a bed. A bed is made of a rectangular wooden frame of two long beams and two short ones. The beams enter holes in four posts called "leshonot" standing at the four corners of the frame (see above 4:2). The posts are set on four legs to raise the bed from the ground, and the legs are called "kera'im".
whose two long sides were removed after it became impure. The two long beams.
and he made new ones for it and did not change the holes. He put in two new beams and did not alter the holes in the posts.
it is still in its impurity. Because the old long sides that were removed can be returned into the holes.
the old ones were broken. Even when they are not attached to the bed.

pure, for everything follows the old ones. Although the bed stands with new long sides, the impurity touched the original bed, whose existence depended on the integrity of the old long sides. Therefore when the old long sides were broken, the old bed is considered dismantled and all its parts are purified.
and a short side was removed. One of the beams of the width of the bed.
and two legs. Two of the legs of the bed.
he cut off two posts of a bed diagonally. And the bed came apart into two parts, each of which has a long side and a short side.

or he cut off two legs a handbreadth by a handbreadth diagonally. He cut a handbreadth from two legs of the bed that are not adjacent to each other, and the bed cannot stand because the legs are not of equal height.
or reduced them to less than a handbreadth. He cut all the legs of the bed and left them less than a handbreadth high.
it is still a primary source of impurity. It is impure with midras, for it is not purified by the breaking of only one long side.

the second long side was broken and he repaired it, it is pure from midras but impure by contact with midras. For it is like a new bed that touched the old bed that was impure with midras (as above 7:12).
he did not manage to repair the first until the second was broken, it is pure. For since both long sides were broken, it was entirely purified and the impurity left it.
this is like one who made another vessel from the fragments of a vessel that became impure etc.. See above 12:1.

if a long side and two legs remained... they become impure. The parts of the bed receive impurity from now on, since they can be used by leaning them against the wall. (And what was said above in halakhah 10, that when a long side and two legs were removed it is pure, speaks of a bed that was already impure with midras, which, since the form of the bed no longer exists, is purified from midras. Kesef Mishneh.)
if he immersed it limb by limb. That he took the bed apart into parts that can receive impurity, such as a long side and two legs or a short side and two legs (Babylonian Talmud, Sukkah 16a).
one who takes apart a bed to immerse it. Because it is large and he cannot immerse it all at once.
one who touches its ropes is pure. Although the ropes are a connection to the bed when it is whole (above 21:6), once he took it apart they are no longer considered a connection.
a chest whose opening is on its side. See above 25:15.

its opening is on top, impure with corpse impurity. And likewise with other impurities except midras, like the law of a receptacle (and all those mentioned in this chapter that become impure with a corpse become impure with other impurities, below halakhah 16).
and that which holds a measure. Whose size is forty se'ah or more.
entirely pure. It does not receive impurity at all (see above 3:1-2).
a trough of two logs etc.. Above 26:7.
like a katedra. A palanquin in which one sits (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 4:3). Some explain that it is enclosed by partitions on three sides (Rash, ibid.).
like a bed. That is long and wide and serves for carrying loads.

and one of stones is entirely pure. Because it is made of stone and has the law of stone vessels, which do not receive impurity (Mifal Mishneh Torah edition, based on Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 24:17). Some explain that this speaks of a cart meant for carrying stones, made like a net with large holes, and it is pure because it cannot hold pomegranates (Rash, Kelim 4:3; see Aruch HaShulchan 231:3).
impure with midras. Because sometimes people lay on it to rest.
and which is played with in the kumpon. Which is used for competitions and training in the camp.
impure with corpse impurity. Because people do not lie on it, but it is impure as a vessel.
and the dilat of the Arabs. A small shield hung for decoration on the walls and ceiling of the house, or used for play (see Commentary to the Mishnah 24:1).
shields. Shields.
the curved shield. A shield shaped like a convex rectangle that surrounds the central part of the body (Tarbut Chomrit, vol. 2 p. 123).
tarbusin. Rolled sheets.
of barbers. On which those having their hair cut sit.
and on which they eat. It serves as a tablecloth (see above 7:1), and is impure because it serves people and utensils like a table (see above 4:1).
footstools. A bench, a stool.
that are before the bed and before the scribes. On which one sitting on the bed or the scribe rests his feet.

of a table. Which is not meant for sitting but for arranging foods on it (Kesef Mishneh). Some explain that the attendant stands on the stool when he wants to take food from the table. It is not impure with midras because its main use is not for that, but it becomes impure with other impurities like the table itself (Sidrei Taharot 211b, based on the Jerusalem Talmud, Shabbat 17b).
and of a cabinet. A base for a cupboard.
entirely pure, because it is like part of the cabinet. For the base of the cabinet is not a vessel in itself but serves the cabinet alone.
writing tablets. Wooden boards fastened to one another (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 24:7).
the folding chair. A folding chair (ibid.).
on which books are placed is impure with midras. Because sometimes the scribe sits on it, so it is also designated for sitting (Mishnah Acharonah, Kelim 24:7).

and of glaziers, in which they place glass vessels, is impure with corpse impurity. For it has the law of flat wooden utensils that serve utensils even when not at work (Shoshanim LeDavid, Kelim 24:8), or it is impure because it has a receptacle (Merkevet HaMishneh).
on which hairnets are laced. They use it to plait nets. It has the law of flat wooden utensils that serve utensils only during work (above 4:1).
large baskets. Woven baskets.
of manure. In which manure is taken out to the fields.
is impure with midras. Because of its size people lean on it to rest (Rash, Kelim 24:9).
of straw is impure with corpse impurity. Like all receptacles.
and the puchlatz of camels. A net of ropes.
and the holes of the netting. The holes of the net.

and it turns out that it has the status of a vessel only for the ropes. Above 3:6 it says that the camel puchlatz receives impurity, so this apparently speaks of a different kind of basket (Meiri, ibid.).
one made for sitting is impure with midras. Above 23:1.
and the dyers' one, in which they place the utensils, is impure with corpse impurity. Like the glaziers' bed (see the explanation above, halakhah 7).
and they cover with it. They cover the grapes with it.
those that hold a measure. See above 24:11.
and of fish skin are entirely pure. For whatever grows in the sea does not receive impurity (above 1:3).
for wrapping utensils. To wrap utensils or clothes in it.
and of straps and of sandals. That are meant to be cut into straps or sandals (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 24:12).
that which is made for lying etc.. See above 23:10.
and of designs. Samples for embroidery (see above 22:8).
for the hands. With which the hands are wiped.
is impure with midras. Because he puts it on the pillow and sleeps on it (Kesef Mishneh, based on the Jerusalem Talmud, Kilayim 9:2).
and of books is impure with corpse impurity. Because sometimes he makes it into a sort of case and puts a Torah scroll on it, or warms his hands with it (Jerusalem Talmud, ibid.).
and of the harps of the Levites. The harps on which the Levites played in the Temple.
is entirely pure, because it is not among the things used by people. For they serve utensils only when not at work.
gloves. Gloves.
and of locust gatherers. Those who hunt locusts for food.
and of fruit gatherers. Those who collect fruit for drying.

is entirely pure, because it is not among the things used by people. Perhaps the purpose of the leather is to protect the fruit from being soiled by the sweat of the hand, and therefore it is not considered among the things people use (see above 7:5).
hairnets. Nets that are placed on the hair.
of a girl are impure with midras. Because it is woven densely and fit for sitting (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 24:16).
and of an old woman are impure with corpse impurity. Because it is not fit for sitting since its holes are large (ibid.).
and which they make for play. See above 22:9.
of a person is impure with midras. Of any material, because it is meant for midras.
of metal and of an animal. An animal's sandal made of metal (Chiddushei HaRambam, Kelim, Bava Batra 2:11; see Kesef Mishneh and Tosefta Kelim p. 77).
of cork and of tzefirah. An animal's sandal made of cork or of woven reed (Kesef Mishneh).
entirely pure. See above 2:7.
was made for another task and serves sitting along with it. That the utensil was made from the start both for work and for sitting.
and anything that becomes impure with midras becomes impure with a corpse... as we have explained. Above 23:1.
and becomes impure with liquids. Which are derivatives of impurity, and the Sages decreed that they make utensils impure (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumah 7:2).
baskets. Woven baskets.
worn out. Worn and weak.
that he patched onto the sound one. He attached it to a whole and strong basket to serve as a patch for it.
for if he punctured it with a hole the size of a pomegranate-passage, both are pure. See Piskim VeShitot.
whose outer sides became impure with liquids. That impure liquids touched their outer side.

their inside did not become impure for terumah. The inside of the vessel does not make terumah impure. For by Torah law liquids do not make utensils impure, only by rabbinic law, and they made a distinction in this case so that terumah and sacrifices would not be burned because of it. All this applies to terumah, but for sacred food the law of the inside of a vessel is like the law of its outside (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumah 7:3-4).
nor their necks. The necks of the vessel.
nor their ears. A projection from the body of the vessel into which the vessel's handle is fitted (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 25:7).
nor their handles. The handles of the vessel.

nor the place of the finger that is sunk into the rim of the vessel. A recess in the thickness of the rim of the vessel into which one puts a finger so as not to put the hand inside the vessel when holding it (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 25:7).
both sackcloth utensils. Those woven from animal hair.
such as sacks and marzufin. Large sacks for storing goods.
and even baskets and large baskets. Woven baskets.
flat utensils. Such as wooden and leather utensils.
since they do not receive impurity by Torah law. See above 4:1.

if their outer sides became impure with liquids their inside did not become impure. Although these utensils have no outside and inside, since they have no receptacle, because they do not receive impurity by Torah law, they distinguished in these utensils between the side of the vessel that is not used and the side that is used, and the law of the side not used is like the law of the outside of a vessel.
those fit for midras. And that receive midras impurity by Torah law.

have no outside and inside. The Sages did not distinguish in them between the side that is used and the side that is not used, and wherever the liquids touched, the whole vessel became impure. For to distinguish between Torah impurity and liquid impurity, which is rabbinic, it suffices to make a mark in receptacles that have a real outside and inside (Babylonian Talmud, Bekhorot 38a).
measures for wine and oil. Measuring vessels.
and the zomei of listra. A utensil with two ends, with a fork at one end and a flat spoon at the other.

have no outside and inside etc.. In ordinary utensils they distinguished between their inside and outside because the way they are used is that the liquid touches their inside and not their outside. But with measures for wine and oil, one draws from the barrel and puts the whole measure into the liquid, so in their way of use the liquids touch both their inside and their outside; likewise with the zomei listra both sides are put into the dish; and with a wine strainer both sides serve the same task (Mishnah Acharonah, Kelim 25:3; see Rash there, who explained differently).
the goad, which is the malmad. A stick with a sort of spear at one end, called a charchur, and at its other end a nail with which the animal is driven, called a darban (above 11:23).

both its ends have an outside and inside. Each of its ends is considered a vessel in itself that has an outside and inside (apparently because it is a large utensil each of whose ends serves a different task; Tiferet Yisrael, Kelim 25:2).

if liquids fell on the charchur, only seven handbreadths of the wood adjacent to the charchur became impure. The charchur is considered the inside of the vessel, and the wood adjacent to it is considered the outside of the charchur and becomes impure with it.

if they fell beyond seven and beyond four etc.. Although the charchur and the darban are considered separate vessels, each with an outside and inside, the goad as a whole is also considered a vessel with an outside and inside: the charchur, the darban and the wood adjacent to them are considered inside, and the middle of the goad is considered outside. Therefore if impure liquids fell there, only the middle of the goad becomes impure, and not the seven handbreadths near the charchur or the four near the darban.
a pouch. Of leather.

but if the outer one extended beyond etc.. Then they are considered one vessel, and the inner vessel is like the inside of the vessel and the outer one like the outside (Chiddushei HaRambam, Kelim, Bava Batra 4:2).

and with a creeping animal, either way, if one of them became impure the other did not become impure. Most commentators read: "if one of them became impure, the other became impure," because with creeping-animal impurity there is no difference whether it became impure from inside or outside (Kesef Mishneh, Maggid Mishneh and others).
one who hollows out a quarter and half a quarter. A block of wood in which he made two hollows to measure a quarter-log and half a quarter-log.

the second did not become impure. For each measure is considered an outside with respect to the other measure, and just as the outside of a vessel that became impure does not make its inside impure, so the measure that became impure does not make the other measure impure.
and when he immerses it, he immerses all of it. For the whole block of wood is one vessel.
and it was boiling. The water was boiling in it.

we do not worry that liquids may have come out of it and touched its outside and returned inside. In which case they would have become impure from the outside of the vessel and then returned and made impure the liquids in the kettle.
pure for terumah. But not for sacred food, for a vessel whose outside became impure makes impure the sacred food inside it (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumah 7:3).
